title: RIPPLE: Differential Testing of Exact-Value Restoration Boundaries in Privacy-Preserving LLM Pipelines
abstract: Privacy-preserving large language model (LLM) pipelines often replace sensitive input values with placeholders before inference and later restore approved values in the generated response. This restoration step can itself introduce unauthorized sensitive values into the final output, yet standard evaluations often conflate values already produced by the model with values newly inserted by restoration. This article presents RIPPLE, a differential regression-testing methodology that attributes exact sensitive-value exposure to either raw model output or downstream restoration. Allow-only policy gating is treated as a baseline restoration obligation rather than as the methodological contribution. RIPPLE separately measures sensitive values present before restoration, values newly released by restoration, and sensitive values visible in the final output; it also distinguishes exact-value non-release from typed marker or placeholder category disclosure. In a matched 120-case attribution probe, RIPPLE distinguishes raw sensitive literals already present in model output from releases caused by placeholder restoration. In a designed 18,000-case controlled benchmark with no pre-existing unauthorized exact values, naive restoration causes unauthorized exact-value release in 78.2% of benchmark cases; this value is a regression-test stress rate for the constructed perturbation suite, not an estimate of deployment incidence. Under the same tested contract, the evaluated policy-gated engines produce zero measured restoration-induced releases. An 11-defect mutation study shows that final-exposure, differential-release, DLP, policy-gating, proxy, and audit signals detect different classes of restoration faults, and a marker/opaque-placeholder analysis shows how generic markers and opaque placeholders remove category-disclosure surfaces without changing exact-release outcomes. Evaluations using a public Gretel PII corpus adaptation and 360 frozen outputs from a Microsoft Presidio–LLM pipeline provide independently sourced synthetic and reproducible downstream checks. RIPPLE is an audit-oriented method for testing exact-value restoration boundaries, not a general privacy or prompt-injection defense.

title: EB-AIOps: Evidence-Bound and Injection-Resilient Intelligent Triage for Cloud Security Logs
abstract: Modern cloud platforms and large distributed systems generate massive volumes of logs that record failures, access behavior, and system states. These logs are central to security monitoring and reliability engineering. While recent log analysis models can detect anomalies with high accuracy, operational triage remains difficult. Security teams still need to manually inspect long log sequences, and emerging LLM-based assistants often produce explanations that lack sufficient evidence. More critically, cloud logs are untrusted inputs, and malicious strings embedded in logs can manipulate automated assistants and trigger unsafe outputs. This paper presents EB-AIOps, an evidence-bound and injection-resilient framework for intelligent cloud security triage. The proposed system integrates structured log parsing, risk-aware incident detection, evidence retrieval, and controlled language-model-based reporting. Only high-risk windows are forwarded for triage. For each suspected incident, the framework retrieves a small set of relevant historical logs and constrains the assistant to generate reports strictly grounded in this evidence. Raw log text is isolated from system instructions, which limits the effect of prompt injection hidden inside logs. Experiments on large-scale distributed log datasets show that EB-AIOps achieves strong detection performance, reaching 0.991 accuracy, 0.984 F1-score, and 0.993 AUC, outperforming deep sequence and transformer-based baselines. The framework also improves cross-system generalization, with F1-scores above 0.93 under domain shift. More importantly, EB-AIOps produces highly grounded triage outputs with 0.97 evidence precision and reduces prompt-injection attack success to 0.04, compared to 0.42 for unconstrained assistants. These results demonstrate that EB-AIOps enables accurate, verifiable, and secure incident triage for real cloud security operations.

title: Semantic Isomorphism Attacks and Defense Evaluation for Jailbreaking Large Language Models
abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) faces persistent challenges from jailbreak attacks. While existing methods mostly leverage prompt engineering or adversarial optimization, we identify and formalize an underexplored semantic isomorphism vulnerability where harmful and safe scenarios share highly consistent underlying operational principles, allowing harmful intent to bypass semantic refusal. We present Safe2Harm, a four-stage semantic isomorphism jailbreak attack framework integrating safe rewriting, topic mapping, safe response generation, and topic inversion. Evaluations on 8 mainstream LLMs and three benchmarks show Safe2Harm substantially outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reaching 99.5% peak ASR on large-parameter models. Further mechanistic and defense analysis reveals the strong input-side stealthiness of the attack, alongside detectable signals in inversion and final outputs, offering key insights for multi-layered LLM safety defense.

title: PIDS-Bench: Evaluating Prompt-Injection Detectors Under Over-Defense, Obfuscation, and Distribution Shift
abstract: Prompt-injection detectors are typically evaluated using aggregate $F_{1}$ on in-distribution test data, which offers limited insight into behavior under distribution shift, particularly on the benign side of the decision boundary, where false positives impose direct operational cost yet are seldom measured. We present PIDS-Bench, a frozen multi-axis benchmark that jointly evaluates attack detection and benign false-positive behavior at fixed thresholds, spanning in-distribution inputs, hard-benign prompts that mimic injection structure without malicious intent, obfuscated attacks, and domain and structural distribution shifts. We evaluate seven detectors (learned baselines, external prompt-injection classifiers, and broad-safety comparators) alongside a rule-based lower-bound reference. Multi-axis evaluation exposes a failure mode that aggregate $F_{1}$ conceals. A detector exceeding $F_{1} = 0.98$ on the held-out split still misclassifies roughly one-third of an externally-sourced benign subset drawn from public corpora and restricted to security-adjacent content. Across a full threshold sweep and five training seeds, no internal detector reaches an operating point satisfying $F_{1} \geq 0.95$ and hard-benign $\mathrm {FPR} \leq 0.10$ together on this stress distribution. Decomposing by provenance, we find that hard-negative augmentation nearly eliminates over-defense on curated stress inputs but leaves it substantially intact on externally-sourced prompts, a pattern we term provenance-sensitive over-defense. The asymmetry holds across both fine-tuned architectures and does not diminish as the augmentation pool grows, with the externally-sourced FPR remaining far above the 0.10 target. Whether augmentation matched to the externally-sourced distribution would close this gap is untested; threshold calibration and curated-style augmentation alone do not.

title: Hybrid Feature Representation and Deep Anomaly Detection for Jailbreak Prompt Defense
abstract: Prompt-based jailbreak attacks remain a practical threat to the safe deployment of large language models, as adversaries can bypass moderation policies using carefully crafted instructions and obfuscation. This paper investigated whether anomaly detection can serve as a lightweight defense for identifying malicious prompts without relying on continuously updated labeled attack sets. Study developed a hybrid feature representation that combined word-level and character-level TF–IDF (Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency) features with embedding vectors, and evaluated TruncatedSVD and PCA for dimensionality reduction. Three anomaly detectors—Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, and a deep autoencoder trained primarily on benign prompts—were assessed on a public prompt-injection dataset using ROC-based threshold selection. The deep autoencoder with SVD achieved the strongest overall performance, reaching 0.94 recall and 0.31 F1-score, while exhibiting a conservative detection behavior with elevated false positives. These results suggest that deep reconstruction-based anomaly scoring can function as a high-recall first-stage safety filter for jailbreak prompt defense, with future improvements focused on calibration to reduce benign misclassifications. Rather than being a stand-alone classifier, the suggested approach is meant to serve as a high-recall, first-stage safety filter to support subsequent moderating techniques. The primary limitation is the false-positive rate, which motivates threshold calibration and layered moderation as future work.

title: Prompt Firewalls for Securing Large Language Model Systems: Threats, Architectures, and Design Trade-offs
abstract: Large Language Models are increasingly deployed as core components of enterprise automation platforms, retrieval-augmented generation systems, and autonomous agentic work-flows. While these systems enable advanced reasoning and decision-making, they also introduce a new attack surface rooted in natural language interaction. Prompt injection and indirect prompt injection attacks exploit the instruction-following behavior of these models, allowing adversaries to manipulate system behavior through untrusted inputs and external context.Prompt Firewalls have emerged as a security mechanism that intercepts and constrain prompt construction before or during model inference. Existing approaches range from lexical filtering and policy enforcement to semantic validation, role-aware parsing, and stateful monitoring across multi-step workflows, each presenting distinct architectural trade-offs.This survey provides a structured and implementation-oriented review of Prompt Firewall research. We examine attack models, design principles, deployment strategies, and enforcement mechanisms, and compare representative approaches to identify strengths, limitations, and open challenges in securing Large Language Model systems.

title: Evil-AI Benchmark: An Evaluation Framework for Adversarial Security Assessment of LLM Agents in Smart Environments
abstract: Smart environments increasingly integrate artificial intelligence (AI) to process sensor data, coordinate Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and actuate cyber-physical services. Within these environments, large language models (LLMs) are emerging as decision-making and interaction components. However, LLM integration expands the attack surface of these environments, and existing benchmarks focus largely on risks associated with text-based interactions and LLM-generated outputs, failing to capture cyber-physical risks that arise when models control physical actuators. This paper introduces Evil-AI Benchmark, an open-source evaluation framework for assessing LLM agents in smart environments through (i) five adversarial threat vectors—prompt injection, persuasion, attacker-in-the-middle (AITM) simulation, data leakage, and unsafe actions—and (ii) a capability validation that checks whether a model can correctly activate device-control tools. The benchmark instruments tool activations and forwards tool-trigger events to an external Arduino-driven servo actuator, providing physical verification of actuation events. To demonstrate the benchmark in practice, we evaluate eight representative LLMs using 350 executable scenarios: 250 adversarial tests spanning five smart-environment domains (smart home, healthcare IoT, industrial control, public infrastructure, and smart building), 50 capability checks, and 50 benign over-refusal tests. Responses are scored by two independent judge models and verified by a human evaluator. We report Evilness as the extent to which attacks succeed. The Evilness Score equals the number of successful attacks, and the Evilness Rate is the corresponding percentage. Across models, Evilness Rates range from 0.8% to 54.0% (2–135 successful attacks out of 250), while Defense Rates range from 46.0% to 99.2%. The most persistent weaknesses occur in persuasion, especially under sustained multi-turn pressure, and in prompt injection. Moreover, larger models are not necessarily more robust against adversarial attacks. We additionally quantify over-refusal on benign authorized requests, so that safety is not rewarded by indiscriminate refusal. Evil-AI Benchmark provides reproducible diagnostics and quantitative metrics that connect text-based safety evaluation with real-world cyber-physical operation.

title: VectorSec: A Web-Based AI Security Scanner for Systematic Evaluation of LLM Vulnerabilities
abstract: The increasing deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) in critical infrastructure has introduced a class of security risks that remain insufficiently characterised and poorly tooled in practice. Attack vectors including prompt injection, jailbreaking, code execution facilitation, covert data exfiltration, and training data poisoning present quantifiable threats to systems that rely on LLM outputs, yet no lightweight, provider-agnostic tool exists to measure these risks systematically. This paper presents VectorSec, an open-source, web-based LLM security scanner built with Python and Dash. The tool executes a structured test suite of 320 adversarial prompts spanning 16 vulnerability categories aligned with the OWASP Top 10 for LLMs. Each response is scored through a four-stage pipeline combining pattern matching, sentiment analysis, semantic similarity, and secondary LLM verification. Evaluation across three open-source models demonstrates that pattern-matching-only filtering misses approximately 15% of High and Critical findings that semantic verification correctly identifies, motivating the multi-layer design. VectorSec provides interactive dashboard reporting, real-time progress tracking, and audit-ready PDF and CSV exports, lowering the barrier to structured LLM security assessment in operational settings.

title: Securing Autonomous Clinical Agents: Time-Scoped Hypergraph Delegation for Controlling Patient Data Access
abstract: Healthcare data breaches cost hospitals and clinics an average of $7.42M USD per breach. Autonomous multi-agent LLM pipelines in clinical settings multiply that exposure structurally: a prompt-injection payload embedded in a laboratory report or referral note traverses the full delegation hierarchy before any human reviewer observes it. Standard mechanisms including flat Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) and Macaroon caveat chains provide no structural guarantee that a spawned sub-agent's permissions remain bounded by its parent's scope. The Minimum Necessary Standard must hold across mixedsensitivity EHR data and multi-hop chains simultaneously. That is, the gap is architectural, not behavioral. We present the Hybrid Scripted-Execution and Prompt-Grounded Injection (SEPI) design, a replay-faithful methodology that freezes authorizationrequest traces and replays them identically across baselines to isolate authorization semantics from LLM stochasticity. Applied to a five-agent post-surgical oncology coordination workflow over a synthetic Electronic Health Record scenario, and evaluated against 39 clinically grounded injection payloads across leafagent, mid-delegate, and parent-orchestrator compromise scenarios, NGAC-hypergraph time-scoped delegation reduces mean sensitivity-weighted blast radius $\left(B_{\mathrm{w}}\right)$ by 75.0% relative to flat RBAC and 65.2% relative to Macaroon caveat chains. A temporal ablation shows that removing $t_{\text{expire }}$ raises mean $B_{\mathrm{w}}$ by 75.0% relative to full NGAC. The reduction follows from structural properties of the delegation architecture: attenuation is provable by construction rather than contingent on model behavior. Across model conditions, Claude Sonnet 4.6 actively detected all 39 payloads while open-source models showed weaker or intermittent behavioral protection, reinforcing authorization as the model-agnostic containment control.

title: SemGuard: A Triple-Anchor Semantic Security Gateway for Multilingual Prompt Attack Detection in Large Language Models
abstract: The threat posed by adversarial prompts to large language models is becoming harder to ignore. Problems including prompt injection, jailbreaking, phishing, and Unicode-based attacks are now widespread. Most existing solutions protect against only one threat type, operate in English only, and provide no explanation for their decisions. We present SemGuard, a multilingual security gateway using Triple-Anchor Semantic Threat Modeling, which simultaneously evaluates each input against three semantic reference sets: attack, safe, and destructive. SemGuard detects four threat types concurrently in Arabic, Arabizi, and English. We expand the original Arabic Security Dataset from 319 to 807 validated examples across seven threat categories, using three independent LLM judges (GPT-4o, Grok-4, Llama 3.3 70B) achieving Fleiss' $\kappa=0.839$. After retraining on the expanded dataset, SemGuard achieves a mean F1-score of 0.989 and recall of 0.991, representing a 13.7% improvement over the original implementation. Analysis of 527 rejected examples reveals quantitative evidence of threat-category ambiguity, with impersonation exhibiting a 98.2% inter-judge disagreement rate, validating the necessity of the Triple-Anchor framework. This work also presents the first Arabic LLM security dataset with a formal LLM-as-Judge annotation protocol.

title: TrustTrace: Provenance-Aware Tracing of Indirect Prompt Injection Propagation in LLM-Assisted Learning Workflows
abstract: Indirect prompt injection can persist through retrieval, generation, and revision after the visible payload disappears. Existing defenses primarily detect suspicious inputs or constrain immediate actions, but they provide less evidence about which source influenced which final-artifact span through a temporally valid route. This paper presents TrustTrace, a provenance-aware framework for source-to-artifact tracing in LLM-assisted learning workflows. TrustTrace constructs a heterogeneous temporal graph over sources, retrieved contexts, prompts, responses, revision operations, and artifact spans. A dual-flow encoder separates legitimate evidence transmission from unauthorized control transmission, while differentiable reachability supports source attribution, contaminated-span localization, activation-stage estimation, and complete-path recovery. A bounded counterfactual verifier performs fact-preserving neutralization, suffix replay, calibrated set-valued attribution, and abstention. The primary pipeline uses procedurally separated GPT-5.5 profiles; construct validity is therefore tested with independent human ratings, a Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct generation set, and an independent Qwen3 neutralization-and-judging stack. On the independently audited EduTrace-IPI subset, TrustTrace improves strict Complete-Path F1@3 from 0.631 to 0.684 over the architecture-matched terminal-supervision baseline and from 0.659 to 0.716 after disagreement-flagged workflows are excluded. Human ratings of 800 stratified artifact spans correlate with the continuous contamination score at Spearman $\rho =0.78$ , and an independent Qwen3 verifier preserves most of the primary result (Span-F1 0.731 and Complete-Path F1@3 0.671). On Qwen3-generated workflows, TrustTrace obtains Span-F1 0.681 and Complete-Path F1@3 0.598 without retraining. Binary detection gains remain comparatively small, and specialized guards remain stronger on selected native input- or action-level metrics. The evidence supports TrustTrace as a complementary forensic layer for calibrated span and path tracing rather than a replacement for preventive defenses.

title: Auditable LLM Safety-Judge Selection via Confidence-Interval Filtering on Unsafe Recall
abstract: Large language model (LLM) safety judges from different model families can disagree by an order of magnitude on the same responses, with reported attack success rate (ASR) ranging from 0.04 to 0.42 on a single benign-only fine-tuned model. This is not ordinary classifier noise: the gap is driven by judges whose unsafe recall is too low to detect harmful outputs. Existing pipelines select judges by aggregate metrics such as balanced accuracy, which can look acceptable while false negatives silently suppress ASR. We propose a confidence-interval (CI) filtered two-stage judge-screening framework. Stage 1 retains only judges whose Clopper–Pearson 95% lower bound on unsafe recall exceeds a predefined floor; Stage 2 selects the highest balanced-accuracy judge among the survivors. When no judge has sufficient calibration evidence, the framework emits an explicit low-confidence or abort verdict, and downstream ASR can be accompanied by a Rogan–Gladen first-order prevalence correction. We evaluate the framework on seven labeled prompt sources and nine candidate judges spanning five base model families in two judge categories. In small-calibration regimes, it reduces the rate of selecting judges that fail the unsafe-recall screen by an order of magnitude. Across five English sources it produces a pass and reject map that is stable under the unweighted bound, with one of 45 judge-source cells reversing under design weighting; on a Chinese multilingual jailbreak source, every English-trained judge fails Stage 1 and the framework abstains. A controlled supervised fine-tuning (SFT) case study with varying benign-to-safety data ratios shows that on the same benign-only (1:0) responses the reported ASR spans a factor of 12.5 across judges, and that the lowest-recall judge underestimates the human-labeled ASR by a factor of 6.0; CI-filtered screening prevents the corresponding ASR underestimation.

title: Evolving Jailbreaks: Automated Multi-Objective Long-Tail Attacks on Large Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in Web-facing applications, raising concerns about jailbreak attacks that bypass ethical and safety constraints. While prior work has demonstrated the effectiveness of automated jailbreaks, most methods operate within conventional natural language distributions, limiting their stealthiness and structural diversity. This paper focuses on long-tail jailbreak attacks, which exploit rare or structured input patterns, such as code-oriented or encryption-style prompts, to evade safety alignment mechanisms. To systematically explore this complex search space, an LLM-assisted evolutionary framework, EvoJail, is proposed. Each candidate prompt is represented as a semantic-algorithmic individual that integrates natural language descriptions with a soft reversible encode-decode mechanism. EvoJail leverages LLMs for initialization, mutation, crossover, and repair of candidates, while a multi-objective evolutionary process jointly optimizes attack success rate and output fluency. Extensive experiments across multiple target models, benchmark datasets, and evaluation metrics demonstrate the competitiveness of EvoJail against existing methods. These results highlight the potential of combining LLM reasoning with evolutionary search for automated discovery of robust long-tail jailbreak prompts.

title: Evaluating Prompt Injection Risk and Guardrails in LLM-Enabled Home IoT Assistants
abstract: Smart home virtual assistants are increasingly powered by large language models to enable information retrieval and home device actuation. As a result, intelligent home environments are becoming more exposed to untrusted inputs, increasing their susceptibility to prompt injection, role confusion, and indirect prompt injection through retrieved context. In this paper, we propose a layered architecture that separates LLM-driven intent interpretation from the authorization and safety enforcement mechanisms governing the managed environment. The architecture is developed and evaluated using an incremental hardening approach, in which a naive baseline system is progressively enhanced with authentication and role tagging, pre-LLM policy enforcement, context sanitization and prompt rewriting, and post-LLM action gating mechanisms. Early findings of a small scenario setting indicate that progressive layered enforcement largely diminishes potential risks whereas post-LLM gating inhibits more complex prompt-based threats even when the language model itself produces unsafe commands. The results are preliminary and are limited to four attack scenarios and one local LLM backend but the model can be generalized to more extensive policies of smart-homes and more complex jailbreak and multimodal attack cases.

title: Whispers of Wealth: A Systematic Red-Teaming Study of the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2)
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are increasingly used to automate financial transactions, but their reliance on contextual reasoning introduces new security risks. The Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) secures agent-mediated purchases through cryptographically signed mandates; however, its robustness against reasoning-layer attacks remains unclear. This paper presents a systematic red-teaming evaluation of AP2 and identifies vulnerabilities arising from prompt injection. Two attack techniques are introduced: the Branded Whisper Attack, which manipulates product ranking through adversarial content, and the Vault Whisper Attack, which induces cross-user data disclosure through crafted prompts. Using a functional AP2-based shopping agent implemented with Gemini-2.5-Flash and the Google Agent Development Kit (ADK), the evaluation demonstrates that indirect prompt injection achieves a 100% success rate in manipulating product ranking, while direct prompt injection leads to cross-account data exposure in 20% of cases. These attacks succeed without breaking cryptographic enforcement, operating entirely through reasoning-layer manipulation. The results reveal a fundamental limitation of agent-mediated payment systems: cryptographic guarantees ensure execution correctness but do not protect decision-making. Securing such systems requires additional mechanisms that constrain how contextual inputs influence agent reasoning.

title: A Survey of Fuzzing Techniques for Large Language Model Agents: Challenges, Methods, and Future Directions
abstract: With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), LLM-based agents are evolving from single-turn text generators into autonomous decision-making systems capable of task planning, tool invocation, memory retrieval, and environmental interaction. However, the openness of agent environments and the nondeterminism of model-driven decision logic introduce security and reliability risks that are difficult to capture with conventional software testing. Fuzzing, as an automated and scalable vulnerability discovery technique, provides a promising approach for assessing the robustness of LLM agent systems. This paper presents a systematic survey of fuzzing techniques for LLM agents. First, we analyze the distinctive architecture of LLM agents and summarize three representative threat categories: indirect prompt injection, planning hallucination, and tool abuse. Second, we review existing fuzzing methods from three perspectives: test-case generation and mutation, environment simulation and interaction monitoring, and test-oracle construction. Particular attention is paid to LLM-enhanced fuzzers that exploit the semantic understanding and generation capabilities of LLMs to improve mutation quality and attack effectiveness. Finally, we connect the main technical challenges with an actionable research roadmap, including semantic coverage, cost-aware execution, reproducible oracles, multi-agent fuzzing, gray-box guidance, and automated repair.

title: A Privacy Preserving Federated XLM-RoBERTa Framework for Multilingual Prompt Injection Defense in Educational AI Platforms
abstract: AI-powered education systems have revolutionized personalized learning, multilingual assistance, and intelligent support in education. Such systems are still susceptible to prompt injection attacks, in which the adversary can submit prompts to the system that cause it to provide unexpected answers, reveal hidden code, or execute unsafe code. In multilingual settings, this risk is magnified even more by code-mixed or cross-lingual prompts, which can be targeted by malicious actors to evade existing countermeasures. In this paper, we introduce a Federated Multilingual Prompt Injection Defense Framework for educational AI systems based on XLM-RoBERTa. The framework uses federated learning to collaboratively train detection models using distributed institutional data that contains no sensitive student or academic information, thus maintaining privacy. XLM-RoBERTa is used because of its high multi-lingual text comprehension and categorization abilities, enabling it to identify malicious prompts across a variety of languages. The proposed system includes real-time screening, anomaly detection, and response filtering to provide a more secure and reliable learning environment in the presence of AI. Both IID and non-IID federated settings are tested with multilingual prompt datasets. The results show that the model achieves good detection performance, good privacy protection and robustness against new prompt injection techniques. By adopting the proposed approach, the security and scalability of next-generation educational AI systems can be ensured.

title: Transferability of the GCG Attack Across LLMs: Correlation with Attention Similarity and Transfer Rate Prediction
abstract: In recent years, LLMs have been increasingly used in various domains and have come to play important roles in those areas. However, jailbreaks have become a serious threat because they circumvent safety alignment built into LLMs and induce harmful or inappropriate outputs. They can also lead to confidential information leakage and assistance with dangerous acts. Therefore, it is important to create a framework that can evaluate LLM vulnerabilities quantitatively to reflect the results into practical operation. In this study, we focus on the GCG (Greedy Coordinate Gradient) attack, which is an optimizationbased jailbreak. We aim (1) to clarify the factors underlying the transferability of the GCG attack across LLMs and (2) to predict their Transfer Rate in advance. First, we defined Attention Similarity based on attention patterns obtained from a set of benign prompts and analyzed its correlation with Transfer Rate of the GCG attack. The results show that Attention Similarity at intermediate layers has a consistently high positive correlation with Transfer Rate, and the same trend is observed even in different data conditions. Furthermore, Transfer Rate relationships based on hidden-state-based index are limited in our setting so that similarity in attention structure is more effective for explaining transferability. Next, we introduced RSS (Random Suffix Sensitivity), which captures the vulnerability of a target model to adversarial suffixes, together with its derived feature. We then proposed TRI (Transferability Risk Index), a Transfer Rate prediction index based on three features: Attention Similarity, model size difference, and RSS-based feature. We conducted training and evaluation on multiple model pairs. The results show that TRI can predict Transfer Rate with a certain level of accuracy using only a small number of features, and its predictive performance does not decline markedly even for unseen target models. By utilizing TRI, we can perform 119 times faster attack transferability estimation compared to direct attack based evaluation.

title: PRISM: A Lightweight Method for Jailbreak Detection via Prompt-Response Semantic Coherence Scoring in LLMs
abstract: Detecting whether a jailbreak attack against a large language model (LLM) has succeeded is a challenging problem in AI security. Existing approaches rely on brittle string matching, expensive LLM-based judges, or task-specific classifiers that often fail to generalize. This paper investigates whether semantic coherence is sufficient to evaluate jailbreak success. In this work, we propose PRISM: Prompt-Response coherence for Identifying jailbreaks via Scoring Method, a lightweight method that models jailbreak detection as a coherence problem between the harmful prompt and the model response. The approach combines multiple semantic similarity signals within an ensemble of classical and simple machine learning models. Training in 3,480 pairs of prompt-responses from AdvBench, HarmBench and Alpaca, PRISM achieves F1 = 0.91 and AUC-ROC = 0.98 in the internal test set. In a held-out validation set of 694 labeled samples never seen during training, it outperforms six baseline attack success estimators, achieving the highest accuracy (0.746) and AUC-ROC (0.840), while being up to $\mathbf{1 6} \times$ faster than LLM-based methods. These results demonstrate that semantic coherence provides a robust and efficient signal for jailbreak detection, significantly reducing the implementation complexity of state-of-the-art approaches.

title: Intelligent prompt injection attack detection using transformer and multi-layer perceptron architectures
abstract: Large language models have been increasingly popular in many jobs in recent years, which has led to both new security challenges and opportunities. The main security concerns we can observe these days is prompt injection, which uses carefully constructed inputs to change the behavior of the model and may lead to violation of people privacy, misuse of data, or unstable systems. This study shows how to classify and identify different type of prompt injection attack types, this include act_as, safe prompts, and jailbreaking. In this research two models were used to detect the type of prompt that are transformers and Multi-layer perceptron (MLP).The hyperparameters were used to get maximum accuracy. The model’s performance was evaluated to see if it could effectively recognize various prompt types. The accuracy of both the models in the multi-classification challenge for identifying various prompt types was 99.0% and 99.3%. The outcomes unequivocally demonstrate the model’s performance in identifying various prompt types.

title: Guarding the Gateway: Securing MCP-Mediated RAG Pipelines Against Injection with the Guru Framework
abstract: The adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) within the context of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) frameworks has revolutionized intelligent information processing, by offering the ability to retrieve knowledge that is accurate, contextually relevant, and up-to-date. However, by integrating Model Context Protocol (MCP) services, the integration of intelligent agents, APIs, plugins and external tools repositories further adds to the interoperability but also exposes to severe security issues like prompt injection, context poisoning and malicious tools manipulation attacks. In this paper, Guru, a security framework for protecting RAG pipelines using semantic anomaly analysis, contextual integrity verification, dynamic trust scoring and adaptive privilege isolation, are proposed. The framework periodically checks for threats from the retrieved content through entropy-based threat detection, checks for trustworthiness of the content by engaging in retrieval ranking based on trust and monitors the interaction of the content by employing interaction dependency monitoring, and then forwards the contextual information to the language model. Through experimental evaluation, it is shown that the proposed framework achieves almost 6–14% higher performance than existing methods in some of the security metrics, including contextual integrity preservation (96.8%), injection resistance (95.9%) and secure interaction stability (96.1%). This proposed framework will allow the secure, scalable and trusted deployment of intelligent retrieval ecosystems in critical enterprise environments.

title: A Gateway-Centric Architecture for Bidirectional Content Moderation in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language model (LLM) applications deployed in regulated and high-risk environments face two coupled runtime risks: input-side prompt injection and output-side content compliance violations. Existing defenses are often either model-centric (alignment or fine-tuning) or application-local (keywords and regex), which limits auditability, policy agility, and cross-model portability. This paper proposes a gateway-centric framework that externalizes safety enforcement into a security side-chain. The framework integrates a unified LLM gateway with an external semantic guardrail service to perform bidirectional inspection before and after model invocation. We formalize the architecture with input-risk and output-compliance functions, define a comprehensive threat model and trust boundary, and present a reproducible evaluation protocol. To validate our approach, a prototype implementation based on LiteLLM and Prisma AIRS was evaluated on a rigorously balanced 2,000-sample adversarial dataset merged from diverse sources, including Deepset, wildjailbreak, and jailbreak-classification. Results demonstrate that the proposed architecture achieves an exceptional balance in detection capability, yielding an F1-score of 0.8322, a recall of 0.8531, and effectively maintaining a low False Positive Rate (FPR), thereby outperforming multiple state-of-the-art baselines including Llama Prompt Guard and Deepset DeBERTa. Furthermore, performance testing confirms practical deployability, showing an average added latency of only 320 ms under a 50-concurrent-user load. The paper concludes by discussing the side-chain advantages over model alignment mechanisms, guardrail bypass risks, and adaptive policy-evolution strategies for enterprise AI governance.

title: Prompt Injection as the New SQL Injection: The Emergence of Attacks on AI Reasoning
abstract: The introduction of Large Language Models (LLMs) into enterprise application pipelines represents both a blessing and a curse — the same versatility in following instructions that enables conversational assistants, code copilots, and autonomous agents also erodes the distinction between trusted instruction and untrusted data. In this paper, we argue that Prompt Injection (PI) follows SQL Injection (SQLi) as a fundamental class of attack on machine learning systems. While SQLi leveraged the absence of distinction between code and data in relation queries, PI leverages the absence of separation between system instruction and contextual data in natural language reasoning. The target domain has shifted from syntactic parsing to semantic interpretation, and classic defenses — escaping, parameterization, and whitelisting — are insufficient because natural language lacks a formal grammar to sanitize. We perform a narrative analysis of relevant peer-reviewed and preprint publications within the period 2023–2026, structured around three major dimensions: (i) the taxonomy of direct and indirect prompt injection attacks, (ii) the tactics that PI employs to overcome defenses provided by Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and guardrails, and (iii) the elevated threat landscape of agentic LLM applications with tool capabilities. We formalize the attacker’s strategic edge through a success rate model and offer comparative studies with SQLi, a severity scale for different modes of operation, and guidance for Chief Information Security Officers (CISOs). Our core thesis is that PI represents a paradigm shift, necessitating defense strategies beyond input sanitization toward workflow isolation and defensive LLMs.

title: Identity and Access Management for Agentic AI: A Zero-Trust Security Framework
abstract: Agentic AI systems act autonomously across services, APIs, and data stores, creating identity and access management (IAM) challenges that traditional perimeter-based security frameworks do not address. Unlike human principals, AI agents spawn sub-agents dynamically, receive instructions from a language model vulnerable to prompt injection, and accumulate permissions through sequential tool calls. These properties invalidate the session-based, role-based access control model that existing IAM tools assume. This paper presents ZT-AgentIAM, a zero-trust security framework for managing AI agent identities and permissions at runtime. The framework defines four core components: dynamic token issuance with cryptographic scope binding, policy-based least-privilege enforcement via OPA Rego rules, behavioral attestation using an isolation forest anomaly detector, and continuous tamper-evident audit logging. We evaluate ZT-AgentIAM against five attack classes on a simulated AutoGen-based multi-agent orchestration environment. The framework achieves a mean attack detection rate of 93.4 percent across all threat categories with a full-pipeline latency overhead of 15.1 ms per request, confirming that zero-trust principles are operationally applicable to agentic AI deployments.

title: Development and Cybersecurity Evaluation of an AI-Based Clinical Decision Support Portal for Blood Gas Analysis and Secure Patient Data Management
abstract: The growing adoption of artificial intelligence in healthcare improves diagnostic accuracy and clinical decision support but also creates significant challenges in protecting sensitive patient data. This paper presents an AI-based clinical decision support portal for blood gas analysis and secure patient data management, designed for the diagnosis of diabetic and hematologic syndromes using arterial blood gas analysis. The portal is implemented as a modular full-stack platform based on ReactJS, Express.js, Sequelize ORM, and PostgreSQL, integrating both local and remote large language models for clinical text interpretation and diagnostic reasoning. The study focuses on secure system architecture and privacy-preserving design for AI-enabled healthcare applications. A comprehensive cybersecurity analysis addresses threats such as unauthorized access, API abuse, credential compromise, prompt injection, and risks of sensitive data leakage during external LLM interaction. To mitigate these risks, a multi-layered security framework is implemented, including JWT-based authentication, role-based access control, encrypted credential storage, rate limiting, secure deployment practices, and network isolation. A local anonymization module removes personally identifiable information before any interaction with external LLM services, significantly reducing privacy risks while preserving the effectiveness of AI-assisted diagnostics. The proposed architecture demonstrates a secure and scalable approach to integrating AI into clinical decision support systems and highlights the importance of combining explainable AI with strong cybersecurity mechanisms in modern digital healthcare.

title: Zero-Shot Prompt Injection Detection via N-gram Pooling of Token-Level Hidden States
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines are vulnerable to prompt injection attacks, where adversaries embed malicious instructions inside retrieved documents. Existing embedding-based detectors rely on mean-pooled sentence vectors, which suppress short injection spans hidden within long benign text — a phenomenon we formalize as semantic dilution. We extract per-token hidden states from a frozen 22M-parameter sentence transformer already present in the pipeline and apply N-gram pooling over sliding windows to localize injection signals. On a controlled chunk-level benchmark (1,575 chunks, Enron corpus), our method achieves AUC=0.901 (95% CI [0.869, 0.930]), with confidence intervals non-overlapping with the mean-pool baseline (AUC=0.808). On the public xTRam1 dataset, zero-shot AUC=0.870 exceeds the supervised baseline of 0.764. All three scoring variants execute at identical CPU latency (≈44ms per 500-character chunk). The method requires no labeled data, no fine-tuning, and no access to the generative LLM at inference time.

title: Specialized Domain Jailbreak Benchmark: Exposing Severe Jailbreak Vulnerabilities in Large Language Models
abstract: Trained on massive volumes of internet-sourced data, Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated tremendous potential across diverse domains and achieved widespread adoption. However, harmful information embedded in such data is difficult to eliminate, leaving LLMs at risk of producing unsafe responses during deployment. Although various alignment strategies and defensive measures have been applied to enhance output safety, jailbreak attacks remain unresolved. Existing jailbreak benchmarks primarily focus on general safety concerns, while harmful prompts in professional domains remain scarce. To address this gap, we employ an auxiliary model to simulate attackers with professional knowledge and construct the Specialized Domain Jailbreak Benchmark (SDJBench), with the goal of assessing the coverage of current LLM safety training. SDJBench comprises malicious prompts across five domains-chemistry, biology, engineering, computer science, and psychology. These prompts are highly specialized and explicitly solicit harmful content. Experiments on a range of LLMs reveal persistent vulnerabilities to malicious use in professional fields, along with model-to-model variation in defensive capabilities. Furthermore, cross-domain analysis reveals fluctuations in individual models' safety performance, underscoring a lack of generalization and robustness in current safety training approaches.

title: Execution-Aware Stage-Wise Evaluation Framework for Indirect Prompt Injection in LLM-Based Email Agents
abstract: Indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks have emerged as a critical security threat to large language model (LLM)-based email agents. However, existing evaluation benchmarks largely rely on simulated environments that cannot verify whether an attack will actually succeed in practice, often determining attack success solely based on tool invocation, which leads to frequent misclassifications of attack outcomes. In this paper, we propose execution-aware stage-wise evaluation (EASE) as an automated framework that quantitatively assesses the vulnerability of email agents to IPI attacks in a realistic environment integrated with the Gmail application programming interface (API) and multiple LLM APIs. EASE automates the entire pipeline of delivering attack emails, triggering the LLM agent, and collecting tool invocation logs, and judges attack success by whether the delivered email actually fulfills the attacker’s intent, using tool invocation only as a proxy baseline. Additionally, EASE’s modular architecture allows new LLMs, defense prompts, and attack datasets to be plugged in or replaced independently, and a Streamlit-based web interface makes the framework accessible to non-developers. To validate EASE’s effectiveness, we conducted 15,336 experiments using 639 attack samples across six LLMs under four defense conditions. The results demonstrate that executing attacks in the live service reveals what proxy-based judgment misses: 13.9% of proxy-judged successes are actually failures when the execution outcome is verified. We also observe that the same defense prompt can paradoxically increase the attack success rate for certain LLMs, underscoring the need for execution-grounded evaluation tools such as EASE. EASE is released as an open-source package on GitHub so that email agent developers and security researchers can adopt it immediately.

title: SecureContext EDU: An Open Source University Assistant using Dual - LLM Architecture
abstract: Chatbots powered by LLMs have become popular due to their scalability and instant reply feature. There can be many security issues associated with LLM-based chatbots, which emerge in the interaction between the LLM-based model and other software components. One major problem is that chatbots can be attacked using prompt injection, jailbreaks, and harmful queries. These attacks can change the chatbot behavior and may lead to wrong answers or leakage of sensitive information. This makes security very important in such systems. Existing methods improve the chatbot performance using techniques like modular design, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and input filtering for security. However, most of these methods use a single model and do not have strong real-time protection, making them weak against advanced attacks. Hence, this work proposes a Dual-LLM architecture where security is handled as a separate component for protection against real time threats. A classification model is designed to check the user input queries using threat categories and a confidence score is evaluated to block the harmful inputs. Only safe queries are sent to the response model, which uses a controlled RAG system to generate accurate answers. The system is built as a step-by-step pipeline combining classification and response generation. The results show an accuracy of 90% in detecting threats which leads to reduction of unsafe responses.

title: Poster: From Assistants to Actors: Deconstructing the Security Implications of Autonomous AI Agents
abstract: The cybersecurity landscape is undergoing a paradigm shift from protecting artificial intelligence (AI) models against adversarial attacks to defending against the AI model acting as an autonomous threat actor. This paper deconstructs the emerging attack surface of Agentic AI-systems capable of planning, multi-step reasoning, and tool execution without peraction human approval. We analyze novel vulnerabilities specific to autonomous agents, including Goal Hijacking via indirect prompt injection, long-term memory poisoning within Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architectures, and Non-Human Identity (NHI) abuse. Drawing upon recent threat intelligence from 2025-2026 and the newly released OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, we systematically categorize the most critical attack vectors facing enterprises today. We further propose a behavioral detection framework designed to identify “Goal Drift” in autonomous systems, addressing scenarios where traditional Identity and Access Management (IAM) and human-in-the-loop controls fail to scale. Our findings highlight an urgent need to redesign trust boundaries for the autonomous enterprise, with particular emphasis on NHI governance and continuous runtime authorization.

title: Security and Assurance Evaluation of RAG-Based AI Assistants in Learning Management Systems: A Pilot Study on Prompt Injection and Data Leakage
abstract: Learning management systems increasingly use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistants to answer questions from course documents, but connecting heterogeneous learning materials to large language models also creates new security risks. This paper presents a pilot security-and-assurance evaluation of an LMS-oriented RAG assistant using Indonesian PDF materials from an Administrasi Jaringan course. We construct a role-aware corpus of 26 PDFs covering public instructional modules, internal staff notes, restricted synthetic-sensitive documents, and poisoned public documents. The benchmark contains 80 queries across benign use, direct prompt injection, indirect prompt injection, and leakage attempts, executed under three profiles: vanilla RAG, prompt-guarded RAG, and retrieval-aware hardened RAG. Across 240 Gemini 2.5 Flash runs, the vanilla profile achieved the highest benign utility score of 1.90 but remained vulnerable, with a direct prompt-injection ASR of 0.35, a leakage rate of 0.15, an unauthorized retrieval rate of 0.90, and a poisoned retrieval rate of 0.90. Prompt guarding reduced direct attack success to 0.05 but left retrieval exposure unchanged. The hardened profile eliminated observed leakage, unauthorized retrieval, and poisoned retrieval, with a modest utility reduction and residual direct-prompt-injection susceptibility. These findings indicate that LMS-RAG assurance should evaluate both answer-level behavior and retrieval-layer exposure.

title: A Systematic Review of Jailbreaking Attacks and Defense Mechanisms in Large Language Models
abstract: This paper is a systematic review of the current situation regarding jailbreaking attacks and defensive against Large Language Models (LLMs). The LLMs have performed very well in the field of software engineering and conversational systems. Nevertheless, regardless of such impressive capabilities, there are general weak points, namely, to prompt injection and jailbreaking attacks. Jailbreaking is the tactically designed control of input prompts to evade safety guardrails to cause adversarial or prohibited outputs. The current paper is proposing a comprehensive taxonomy that splits attacks into target visibility: White-Box, attack seeks the exploitation of inner architecture on the basis of gradient or logit exposure, and Black-Box, where the mechanisms of attack are grounded in prompt engineering and linguistic obfuscation. There are also the division of defense methods to Prompt-Level (pre-processing filtering) and Model-Level (intrinsic safety alignment). The findings describe the mathematical concepts of optimization-based attacks, including Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) and inroads into novel deep learning-based advanced alignment models, including Deep Refusal. This proceeds on the background of emphasizing an everlasting adversarial arms race enabled by the current trade-off between robustly helpful and ultra-safe standards of the LLM and further underscoring the ultimate significance of defenses that are robustly anti-out-of-distribution (OOD) attack vectors.

title: Secure MCP-Based Tool-Augmented RAG for Industrial IoT Diagnostics Under Indirect Prompt Injection, Retrieval Poisoning, and Modality Outages
abstract: Industrial IoT diagnostics require integrating diverse evidence streams, such as telemetry, event logs, configuration snapshots, and operational knowledge bases, while adhering to safety and security requirements. Tool-augmented retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) facilitates this integration by merging retrieval processes with the regulated use of tools. In Operational Technology (OT) settings, two primary risks associated with deployment are: (i) indirect prompt injection through retrieved materials or tool outputs, which can disrupt the model context and result in behavior that contradicts established policies; and (ii) limited visibility caused by tool failures, gaps in telemetry, and delayed logging, which diminishes evidential support and raises the chances of producing unsubstantiated outputs. This paper examines a protocol-aligned architecture that integrates MCP-exposed tools within a defense-in-depth RAG pipeline. The approach employs hybrid retrieval and reranking, instruction-aware content filtering, typed least-privilege tool mediation with audit logging, evidence-bound generation with citation enforcement, and outage-aware abstention policies. An OT-oriented stress-test suite is defined based on prior RAG security evaluations, and utility, security, and degradation metrics are reported using a proprietary multi-site IIoT dataset. The findings indicate the importance of treating retrieval and tool interfaces as distinct security boundaries in industrial diagnostic assistants.

title: An Expert-Guided Architecture for Modular and Multi-Client Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) applications increasingly rely on multi-agent and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) architectures to solve complex, knowledge-intensive tasks. However, when deployed as generic platforms serving multiple customers and heterogeneous user groups, existing systems often rely on agent-level routing and prompt hardcoding, leading to poor modularity, limited reuse, and weak controllability. In particular, current approaches lack an explicit abstraction for modeling system capabilities and controlling which capabilities are accessible to different users. We propose an expert-guided multi-agent architecture that separates execution from capability modeling. Agents are responsible for LLM interaction and tool execution, while experts represent indivisible business or task capabilities and guide agent orchestration through dynamic prompt injection. This design enables a generic, multi-instance system in which different customer deployments and user groups share the same agent implementations while exposing different capability sets at the business level. The architecture enforces strong guarantees in terms of answerability, traceability, and controllability. A first working implementation has been developed, and an open-source release is currently in preparation.

title: RUBEN: Rule-Based Explanations for Retrieval-Augmented LLM Systems
abstract: This paper demonstrates RUBEN, an interactive tool for discovering minimal rules to explain the outputs of retrieval-augmented large language models (LLMs) in data-driven applications. We leverage novel pruning strategies to efficiently identify a minimal set of rules that subsume all others. We further demonstrate novel applications of these rules for LLM safety, specifically to test the resiliency of safety training and effectiveness of adversarial prompt injections.

title: Designing AI Agents for Personal Assistance: Human Perceptions and Design Considerations
abstract: Large language models enable agentic workflows that can draft emails, propose calendar meetings, extract tasks from messages, and summarize long documents. Yet, deploying such agents in personal information management raises practical and ethical challenges: users must remain in control, privacy-sensitive data must be minimized, and the system must be transparent about what it did and why. This paper presents a human-centered design for a “Personal Assistant Agent” that orchestrates specialized AI agents for email, calendar scheduling, task management, and summarization while enforcing an explicit Approve/Edit/Reject decision loop. We combine related work on agentic LLM systems with perception-driven requirements, describe an end-to-end architecture including policy checks, consent management, audit logging, and defenses against prompt injection, and present evaluation checks plus a protocol to measure trust, usefulness, and reliability boundaries in realistic workflows.

title: A Gradient-Calibrated Adversarial Prompt Optimization Framework for Large Language Model Safety Evaluation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) may still produce unsafe responses under optimized adversarial prompts, even after safety alignment. Existing gradient-based jailbreak evaluation methods usually use raw gradient signals for discrete prompt search, but raw gradients may be unstable in both magnitude and direction. This paper proposes a gradient-calibrated adversarial prompt optimization framework for LLM safety evaluation. The framework adopts REINFORCE-style randomized discrete prompt optimization as the parent objective and inserts a unified calibration interface before gradient-derived token-search signals are used. We instantiate this interface with two complementary primitives: LSGM for layer-wise magnitude calibration and LiLA for representation-space directional calibration. Experiments on HarmBench show that joint calibration improves attack success rate on multiple open-source safety-aligned models. Ablation results further suggest that the two primitives are more stable when used jointly than when used alone. The framework provides a compact white-box diagnostic tool for analyzing gradient quality in discrete adversarial prompt optimization, while transfer and defense results reveal clear limitations in generalizability and practical robustness.

title: Ai SecureDataGuard: A Big Data Security, Privacy-Preserving and Visualization System for LLM-Powered Smart Homes
abstract: Now large language models and that multi-agent frameworks are widely used, platforms like MOSS can let users talk to smart homes naturally and link up all kinds of household devices. But there’s a slew of tough issues hindering these products from practical commercial application IoT data from every device, constant user privacy leaks, intentional prompt injection and safety guardrail evasion attacks, plus no tool to monitor all risks instantly.For the resolution of all aforementioned drawbacks, I built a complete big data security framework named SecureDataGuard. It packs malicious input screening, differential privacy, federated lightweight anomaly tracking and real-time data visual monitoring into one set of tools. I built the whole system on top of MOSS AI’s multi-agent structure, and also adopted mature industrial AI security tools from Anquan Data Intelligence.First, I made a two-step intent recognition algorithm to block prompt injection and jailbreak attempts. Second, I put together a mixed privacy protection scheme, so we can use data normally without exposing raw user information. I also developed a slimmed-down Transformer model called LADT to catch abnormal device behaviors the second they happen. On top of that, I built a monitoring panel with StarRocks and ECharts, so administrators can track every risk across bird’s-eye view of the whole system.A large set of empirical experiments was implemented with real-world smart home operation records to corroborate the system’s performance.. Encouraging results are observed in our experiments. The system accurately recognizes user commands with an accuracy rate of 97.8%.Identifies anomalous activity within 18 ms and lowers privacy leakage probability by 92%. All 18 key security metrics on the dashboard update within milliseconds. This work delivers a practical, deployable technical solution to handle smart home data safety, privacy risks, Anomalous Event Detection and Visual Risk Control

title: Securing LLM Software Supply Chains: A Layered Lifecycle Framework with Hybrid Post-Quantum Artifact Signing
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in production systems, creating complex development and deployment pipelines that resemble modern software supply chains. These pipelines span dataset ingestion, training workflows, model artifacts, distribution registries, inference infrastructure, and downstream application integration. While prior work has extensively examined model-centric threats such as extraction, inversion, and prompt injection, the security of the complete LLM lifecycle remains insufficiently addressed.Existing software supply chain frameworks, including Sigstore, in-toto, Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA), and The Update Framework (TUF), provide strong guarantees for artifact integrity and provenance. However, these mechanisms were designed primarily for conventional software artifacts and do not fully capture AI-specific lifecycle threats such as data poisoning, training pipeline compromise, and retrieval-augmented prompt manipulation. In addition, most artifact signing infrastructures rely on classical cryptography that may face long-term risk from quantum adversaries.This paper proposes a layered security framework for LLM software supply chains. The framework models LLM security as a lifecycle control problem spanning five layers: Data, Training, Model, Inference, and Application. For each layer, the framework identifies representative assets, threat classes, and defensive controls. The paper further analyzes the role of hybrid post-quantum signatures combining classical digital signatures with post-quantum schemes such as ML-DSA to strengthen artifact integrity at the model distribution stage.To complement the conceptual framework, we include a prototype-oriented evaluation describing how the proposed controls can be instantiated in a reproducible pipeline and quantify the practical overhead of hybrid post-quantum artifact signing. The proposed framework provides a structured model for analyzing threat propagation across the LLM lifecycle while remaining compatible with established supply chain technologies. We contribute a formal threat taxonomy, a comparative analysis against existing frameworks, and an evidence-informed evaluation demonstrating why artifact integrity alone is insufficient for securing LLM supply chains.

title: Research on Dynamic Security Intervention and Semantic Robustness Detection Mechanism of Large Language Models for Sensitive Fields
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed in sensitive domains face several critical challenges, including the difficulty of identifying advanced implicit attacks, the excessive rigidity of existing defense mechanisms, and the insufficient adversarial robustness of underlying detectors. To address these issues, this paper proposes a dynamic safety intervention and robust detection mechanism driven by continuous risk scores. First, we construct a semantically enhanced risk detection model and conduct an in-depth empirical analysis of the optimization challenges under diverse adversarial training baselines (FGSM, PGD, and FreeLB), establishing a front-end risk detector with high precision and a near-zero false-positive rate under small-sample conditions. Second, we design a four-stage risk-adaptive dynamic intervention policy that automatically maps the continuous risk scores produced by the detector to generation-time decoding controls, including temperature reduction and nucleus-sampling (top-p) space contraction, thereby enabling a smooth transition from flexible parameter compression to rigid blocking. Furthermore, we extend the framework to mitigate cross-turn semantic cumulative risk, successfully intercepting progressive multi-turn jailbreak attacks via a cumulative threshold operator. Experimental results on the public HarmBench dataset and a self-built dataset show that the front-end semantic detector achieves an F1 score of 0.9916 with a near-zero false-positive rate, effectively identifying various complex implicit attacks. In safety evaluations, the adaptive policy achieves the highest predefined balanced score in the tested cross-model setting, while the results also show clear backend-dependent variations, achieving balanced scores of 0.94–0.99 and compressing the unsafe proxy to 0.02–0.12, which demonstrates certain architecture-agnostic generalization. System overhead analysis further indicates that the introduced intervention mechanism accounts for less than 4% of the total end-to-end latency, proving highly viable for real-world deployment in highly regulated, high-concurrency sensitive applications.

title: LLM Security Defense Using Unsupervised Learning and Deep Reinforcement Learning
abstract: With the widespread deployment of large language models (LLMs) in intelligent systems, security threats such as prompt injection, jailbreaking, data poisoning, and hidden backdoor attacks have become increasingly severe. Traditional rule-based filtering and static detection methods are unable to capture implicit semantic attacks and hidden-space anomalies, and lack adaptability to evolving adversarial behaviors. To address these challenges,, unsupervised feature learning, deep reinforcement learning, and human-computer interaction. The framework leverages contrastive unsupervised feature learning to mine hidden-space anomalies in multi-modal inputs (text, images, and video), and employs proximal policy optimization (PPO)-based deep reinforcement learning to implement adaptive runtime defense strategies. A multi-modal dataset AISafe-36M is constructed to support the validation of implicit attack detection, jailbreaking interception, and cross-modal robustness. Extensive experiments show that the proposed method achieves 94.8% accuracy in implicit anomaly detection, reduces the attack success rate (ASR) of jailbreaking to below 1.6%, and maintains an average end-to-end latency of 28 ms, fully meeting the performance requirements of industrial applications. The framework realizes the organic integration of computer vision, deep learning, and security defense, and provides a systematic solution for the secure deployment of large language models.

title: An Empirical Evaluation of Prompt Injection Vulnerabilities in Large Language Models Across Multilingual and Obfuscated Attack Scenarios
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly evolved, transforming industries by automating complex tasks and generating human-like content. However, as their adoption accelerates, prompt injection vulnerabilities have become increasingly apparent. Malicious actors exploit these weaknesses to generate phishing emails, deceptive websites, and malware, posing serious security risks. This paper presents an empirical evaluation of six state-of-the-art LLMs (DeepSeek, GPT, Gemini, Grok, Llama, and Qwen) under diverse adversarial prompt scenarios, including direct and multi-stage obfuscated attacks across multiple languages and character encodings. The proposed framework measures how effectively current LLMs resist manipulation into performing harmful actions. Our findings reveal systematic vulnerabilities across all tested models. Even direct prompt injections frequently induce the generation of phishing content, websites, and malware, while elaborate prompts achieve even higher malicious compliance rates, particularly for phishing. Models such as DeepSeek, Gemini, and Grok show especially high susceptibility under complex instructions. Notably, non-English languages consistently exhibit higher compliance rates than English, exposing significant gaps in multilingual safety alignment. Although simple character encodings reduce malicious outputs, they do not eliminate them. These results highlight persistent challenges in LLM safety and underscore the urgent need for stronger defenses and improved security mechanisms to support the ethical and secure deployment of LLMs in cybersecurity sensitive contexts.

title: EB-AIOps: Evidence-Bound and Injection-Resilient Intelligent Triage for Cloud Security Logs
abstract: Modern cloud platforms and large distributed systems generate massive volumes of logs that record failures, access behavior, and system states. These logs are central to security monitoring and reliability engineering. While recent log analysis models can detect anomalies with high accuracy, operational triage remains difficult. Security teams still need to manually inspect long log sequences, and emerging LLM-based assistants often produce explanations that lack sufficient evidence. More critically, cloud logs are untrusted inputs, and malicious strings embedded in logs can manipulate automated assistants and trigger unsafe outputs. This paper presents EB-AIOps, an evidence-bound and injection-resilient framework for intelligent cloud security triage. The proposed system integrates structured log parsing, risk-aware incident detection, evidence retrieval, and controlled language-model-based reporting. Only high-risk windows are forwarded for triage. For each suspected incident, the framework retrieves a small set of relevant historical logs and constrains the assistant to generate reports strictly grounded in this evidence. Raw log text is isolated from system instructions, which limits the effect of prompt injection hidden inside logs. Experiments on large-scale distributed log datasets show that EB-AIOps achieves strong detection performance, reaching 0.991 accuracy, 0.984 F1-score, and 0.993 AUC, outperforming deep sequence and transformer-based baselines. The framework also improves cross-system generalization, with F1-scores above 0.93 under domain shift. More importantly, EB-AIOps produces highly grounded triage outputs with 0.97 evidence precision and reduces prompt-injection attack success to 0.04, compared to 0.42 for unconstrained assistants. These results demonstrate that EB-AIOps enables accurate, verifiable, and secure incident triage for real cloud security operations.

title: Multi-dimensional Vulnerability Analysis of LM Safety Guards via Role-Goal-Format Decomposition
abstract: Current safety guard models for Large Language Models (LLMs) often fail to block complex Jailbreaking attacks because they focus on the structure of a prompt rather than its true intent. To evaluate this problem, we introduce the Role-Goal-Format (RGF) framework, which analyzes how the combination of a user’s persona, their objective, and the text format can bypass safety filters. We compared two small safety guard models: Prompt Guard 2 and Llama Guard 3. The results show that even with the same overall accuracy, they have completely opposite weaknesses. Prompt Guard 2 is easily bypassed by unusual text formats. On the other hand, Llama Guard 3 lacks semantic understanding, missing 76.7% of virus-related attacks. Furthermore, both models exhibit a common vulnerability to contextual breaking; they fail to activate safety alignment when harmful objectives are framed within authoritative and benign personas, such as Teacher, Engineer, and Investigator. These findings highlight that small safety guard models have clear limitations and require multi-layered defenses that understand both text structure and actual intent.

title: LLM Shield: Detecting and Mitigating Adversarial Prompt Attacks on Large Language Models Using Machine Learning
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed multiple domains, including education, cybersecurity, healthcare, robotics, and the Internet of Things (IoT), by enabling natural communication, contextual understanding, and intelligent automation. As these models are increasingly embedded into many software applications, robotics, and connected systems, ensuring their robustness and trustworthiness has become critical. However, most existing research focuses on LLM performance, optimization, and applications, with limited attention to security vulnerabilities and adversarial threats. Emerging attacks such as jailbreaking, prompt injection, and multi-turn manipulation can override safety mechanisms and induce unintended or harmful behavior, posing serious risks to users and systems that rely on LLMs. This study addresses this gap by developing and analyzing a comprehensive dataset of different prompts, including safe and adversarial examples, collaboratively generated mostly by human experts and some by state-of-the-art LLMs such as GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Using TF-IDF feature extraction and multiple machine learning classifiers, including K-Nearest Neighbors, Decision Tree, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Naïve Bayes, Support Vector Machine (SVM), and an ensemble model, we trained our system to automatically detect adversarial intent in LLM prompts. The SVM model achieved the best performance with 99.85% accuracy, 99.87% F1-score, 99.84% Precision, and 99.91% Recall, indicating excellent discriminatory capability. Complementary linguistic, sentiment, and structural analyses revealed that adversarial prompts typically exhibit longer sentence structures, lower lexical diversity, and negative or neutral sentiment, along with manipulative n-gram patterns designed to bypass restrictions. To translate these findings into practice, we designed and implemented LLM Shield, a real-time web platform that monitors, classifies, and alerts users about potential adversarial prompts across connected systems and APIs. The platform visualizes threat types, injection frequencies, and system health through an interactive dashboard. Additionally, LLM Shield utilizes Claude 3.5 Sonnet for linguistic and contextual breakdowns and analyses of detected adversarial prompts. Together, this research contributes an empirical and practical foundation for detecting, mitigating, and monitoring adversarial attacks on LLMs, advancing the development of secure and resilient AI-driven ecosystems.

title: A Four-Axis Systematization of AI and Cybersecurity in the Era of Large Language Models
abstract: The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and cybersecurity has created a complex ecosystem of capabilities and threats. We systematize this space along four axes: AI-for-Cyber, Cyber-for-AI, LLM-for-Cyber, and Cyber-for-LLMs. Using a PRISMA-guided review of 422 recent works, we develop a unified taxonomy of AI–cyber interactions. AI-for-Cyber enables anomaly detection, intrusion detection, vulnerability analysis, and automated response. Cyber-for-AI highlights threats such as data poisoning, model extraction, and privacy leakage. Cyber-for-LLMs exposes vulnerabilities including prompt injection and jailbreaking, while LLM-for-Cyber introduces reasoning-driven capabilities for threat intelligence and offensive operations. We further identify compound cross-axis threats, where attackers combine techniques across axes (e.g., LLM-generated attacks exploiting AI defenses). This Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) consolidates fragmented literature, highlights systemic risks, and outlines open challenges for securing AI-enabled cyber systems.

title: Beyond Wireless Security: Covert Communications in Large Language Model-Enabled Edge Networks
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-enabled edge networks (LLMENs) offer mobile users high-quality and low-latency AI-generated content services in the 6G era. However, unlike typical edge networks, LLMENs present unique security challenges due to the inherent complexity of LLMs, their high computational overhead, and continuous interactions with users. Specifically, both frequent user interactions (i.e., queries and responses) over wireless channels and potential electromagnetic information leakage from intensive LLM computations make LLMENs susceptible to various security threats, such as eavesdropping, jamming, prompt poisoning, and prompt injection attacks. Since existing countermeasures against these attacks often incur prohibitive overhead, developing holistic, efficient, and secure privacy protections for LLMENs is crucial. This article first reviews the vulnerabilities of LLMENs, outlines various attacks, and analyzes the drawbacks of existing countermeasures. To overcome these limitations, we propose a covert communications (CC) and computations approach to enhance both the overall security and efficiency of LLMENs. Furthermore, various supplementary solutions are developed to improve the covertness of this framework. Finally, our approach is further evaluated through a case study where the total latency is minimized under stringent communication and computational security requirements. Numerical results demonstrate the proposed approach's effectiveness in enhancing both privacy protection and the execution efficiency of LLM tasks.
