title: When AI Meets the Web: Prompt Injection Risks in Third-Party AI Chatbot Plugins
abstract: Prompt injection attacks pose a critical threat to large language models (LLMs), with prior work focusing on cutting-edge LLM applications like personal copilots. In contrast, simpler LLM applications, such as customer service chatbots, are widespread on the web, yet their security posture and exposure to such attacks remain poorly understood. These applications often rely on third-party chatbot plugins that act as intermediaries to commercial LLM APIs, offering non-expert website builders intuitive ways to customize chatbot behaviors. To bridge this gap, we present the first large-scale study of 17 third-party chatbot plugins used by over $\mathbf{1 0, 0 0 0}$ public websites, uncovering previously unknown prompt injection risks in practice. First, 8 of these plugins (used by 8,000 websites) fail to enforce the integrity of the conversation history transmitted in network requests between the website visitor and the chatbot. This oversight amplifies the impact of direct prompt injection attacks by allowing adversaries to forge conversation histories (including fake system messages), boosting their ability to elicit unintended behavior (e.g., code generation) by $\mathbf{3}-\mathbf{8} \times$. Second, 15 plugins offer tools, such as web-scraping, to enrich the chatbot's context with website-specific content. However, these tools do not distinguish the website's trusted content (e.g., product descriptions) from untrusted, third-party content (e.g., customer reviews), introducing a risk of indirect prompt injection. Notably, we found that $\sim \mathbf{1 3 \%}$ of e-commerce websites have already exposed their chatbots to third-party content. We systematically evaluate both vulnerabilities through controlled experiments grounded in real-world observations, focusing on factors such as system prompt design and the underlying LLM. Our findings show that many plugins adopt insecure practices that undermine the built-in LLM safeguards.

title: Hijacking Large Audio-Language Models via Context-Agnostic and Imperceptible Auditory Prompt Injection
abstract: Modern Large audio-language models (LALMs) power intelligent voice interactions by tightly integrating audio and text. This integration, however, expands the attack surface beyond text and introduces vulnerabilities in the continuous, high-dimensional audio channel. While prior work studied audio jailbreaks, the security risks of malicious audio injection and downstream behavior manipulation remain underexamined. In this work, we reveal a previously overlooked threat, auditory prompt injection, under realistic constraints of audio data-only access and strong perceptual stealth. To systematically analyze this threat, we propose AudioHijack, a general framework that generates context-agnostic and imperceptible adversarial audio to hijack LALMs. AudioHijack employs sampling-based gradient estimation for end-to-end optimization across diverse models, bypassing non-differentiable audio tokenization. Through attention supervision and multi-context training, it steers model attention toward adversarial audio and generalizes to unseen user contexts. We also design a convolutional blending method that modulates perturbations into natural reverberation, making them highly imperceptible to users. Extensive experiments on 13 state-of-the-art LALMs show consistent hijacking across 6 misbehavior categories, achieving average success rates of 79%–96% on unseen user contexts with high acoustic fidelity. Real-world studies demonstrate that commercial voice agents from Mistral AI and Microsoft Azure can be induced to execute unauthorized actions on behalf of users. These findings expose critical vulnerabilities in LALMs and highlight the urgent need for dedicated defense.

title: SoK: Robustness in Large Language Models against Jailbreak Attacks
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success but remain highly susceptible to jailbreak attacks, where adversarial prompts that coerce models into generating harmful, unethical, or policy-violating outputs. Such attacks pose real-world risks, eroding safety, trust, and regulatory compliance in high-stakes applications. Although a variety of attack and defense methods have been proposed, existing evaluation practices are inadequate, often relying on narrow metrics like attack success rate that fail to capture the multidimensional nature of LLM security. In this paper, we present a systematic taxonomy of jailbreak attacks and defenses and introduce Security Cube, a unified, multidimensional framework for comprehensive evaluation of these techniques. We provide detailed comparison tables of existing attacks and defenses, highlighting key insights and open challenges across the literature. Leveraging Security Cube, we conduct benchmark studies on 13 representative attacks and 5 defenses, establishing a clear view of the current landscape encompassing jailbreak attacks, defenses, automated judges, and LLM vulnerabilities. Based on these evaluations, we distill critical findings, identify unresolved problems, and outline promising research directions for enhancing LLM robustness against jailbreak attacks. Our analysis aims to pave the way towards more robust, interpretable, and trustworthy LLM systems. Our code is available at Code.

title: Parasites in the Toolchain: A Large-Scale Analysis of Attacks on the MCP Ecosystem
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated with external systems through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which standardizes tool invocation and has rapidly become a backbone for LLM-powered applications. While this paradigm enhances functionality, it also introduces a fundamental security shift: LLMs transition from passive information processors to autonomous orchestrators of taskoriented toolchains, expanding the attack surface, elevating adversarial goals from manipulating single outputs to hijacking entire execution flows. In this paper, we identify and characterize a systematic privacy-leakage attack pattern, termed Parasitic Toolchain Attacks, instantiated as MCP Unintended Privacy Disclosure (MCP-UPD). These attacks require no direct victim interaction; instead, adversaries embed malicious instructions into external data sources that LLMs access during legitimate tasks. Unlike traditional prompt injection and tool poisoning attacks, our attack targets the interconnected toolchain itself, assembling multiple legitimate tools into a coordinated workflow whose combined behavior accomplishes malicious objectives. In MCP-UPD, the malicious logic infiltrates the toolchain and unfolds in three phases: Parasitic Ingestion, Privacy Collection, and Privacy Disclosure, culminating in stealthy exfiltration of private data. Our root cause analysis reveals that MCP lacks both context-tool isolation and least-privilege enforcement, enabling adversarial instructions to propagate unchecked into sensitive tool invocations. To assess the severity, we design MCP-SEC and conduct the first large-scale security census of the MCP ecosystem, analyzing 12,230 tools across 1,360 servers. Our findings show that the MCP ecosystem is rife with real-world exploitable gadgets and diverse attack methods, underscoring systemic risks in MCP platforms and the urgent need for defense mechanisms in LLM-integrated environments.

title: AttnTrace: Contextual Attribution of Prompt Injection and Knowledge Corruption
abstract: Long-context large language models (LLMs), such as GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and Claude-Sonnet-4, are increasingly used to empower advanced AI systems, including retrievalaugmented generation (RAG) systems and autonomous agents. In these systems, an LLM receives an instruction along with a context-often consisting of texts retrieved from a knowledge database, memory, or the Internet-and generates a response that is contextually grounded by following the instruction. Many recent studies showed that these LLM-empowered systems are vulnerable to prompt injection and knowledge corruption attacks, where an attacker can inject malicious texts into the context such that the LLM generates an output as the attacker desires. One important research question is how to trace back to these malicious texts from a long context in leading to the attacker-desired output of the LLM. While significant efforts have been made, state-of-the-art solutions still achieve a sub-optimal performance and/or incur high computation cost. In this work, we propose AttnTrace, a new context traceback method based on the attention weights produced by an LLM for a prompt. To effectively utilize attention weights, we introduce two techniques designed to enhance the effectiveness of AttnTrace, and we provide theoretical insights for our design choice. We also perform a systematic evaluation for AttnTrace. The results demonstrate that AttnTrace is more accurate and efficient than existing state-of-the-art context traceback methods. We also show AttnTrace can improve state-of-the-art methods in detecting prompt injection under long contexts through the attribution-before-detection paradigm. As a real-world application, we demonstrate that AttnTrace can effectively pinpoint injected instructions in a paper designed to manipulate LLM-generated reviews. The code and data are available: https://github.com/Wang-Yanting/AttnTrace.

title: Lineage: A UMA2.0 Protocol Extension for Multi-Hop LLM Agent Delegation
abstract: Autonomous Large Language Model (LLM) agents in enterprise and compliance-sensitive systems delegate authority to sub-agents to decompose complex tasks. OAuth 2.0 and User-Managed Access (UMA) 2.0 support delegated authorization between a single requesting party and a resource server, but they lack primitives for the multi-hop authority propagation typical of agent chains. This produces ad hoc permission models and audit gaps incompatible with regulations such as the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA). This paper presents Lineage, an authorization architecture that extends UMA 2.0 with a cryptographically verifiable delegation-chain primitive: every protected request carries a signed record of its full delegation ancestry, validated at the resource server without an additional authorization-server round-trip. Scope monotonicity and bounded delegation depth are enforced by construction, and every authorization decision is recorded in a tamper-detecting audit log. These properties directly implement the technical controls that DORA Article 9 mandates: least-privilege access (Art. 9(4)(c)), data integrity and authenticity (Art. 9(2)), and continuous ICT monitoring (Art. 9(1)). Full DORA compliance requires broader institutional governance beyond any software protocol; Lineage addresses the protocol-layer subset. We validated the design end-to-end on a reference implementation running live LLM agents under DORA-representative scenarios. One test involved an active prompt-injection attempt; the protocol layer blocked it independently of model behavior, which is precisely the property a deployment operator needs to rely on. Per-request overhead remained negligible relative to the UMA baseline. Lineage maintains full OAuth 2.0 and UMA 2.0 conformance. It extends an existing resource server with two chain-signing endpoints and a signing secret, requiring no changes to the authorization server or the UMA token flow.

title: Sentinel-Math: A Framework for Neural Intent Monitoring and SafetyCircuit-Breaking Against Semantically Disguised Logical Tasks in LLMs
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) advance in complex reasoning, they increasingly exhibit "Strategic Dishonesty" against high-order attacks that wrap harmful semantics within mathematical logic. Consequently, traditional black-box filters easily fall into "Safety Hallucinations" or trigger the "Calculator Paradox" by honestly outputting dangerous parameters. To address this, we propose Sentinel-Math, a decoupled intent auditing and safety circuit-breaking framework. Pioneering a neuro-symbolic hybrid mechanism, it utilizes a Risk Sentinel for dynamic dispatching, an external symbolic engine to anchor objective logical truth, and an internal state probe (via Mechanistic Interpretability) to quantify subjective deceptive intents. Our core innovation is a 3D Orthogonal Decision Space {X1, X2, X3}that completely decouples contextual harmfulness, subjective deceptiveness, and objective incorrectness. This eliminates the Calculator Paradox while enabling fine-grained motive diagnosis. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that Sentinel-Math suppresses Jailbreak Success Rates on high-order benchmarks (e.g., EvilMath) below 5.0%, achieves absolute interception against explicit malicious requests, and preserves native mathematical reasoning capabilities (performance drop<0.5%), offering a paradigm for externally guided yet behaviorally endogenous honest AI.

title: PolyJailbreak: Cross-Modal Jailbreaking Attacks on Closed-Box Multimodal LLMs
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have become integral to a wide range of real-world applications by jointly reasoning over text and visual inputs. However, despite recent advances in safety alignment, MLLMs remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, where carefully crafted inputs can bypass safety mechanisms and elicit harmful responses. In this work, we investigate the security vulnerabilities of MLLMs in text-vision scenarios and propose a novel closed-box jailbreak framework, named PolyJailbreak. We first identify a phenomenon, termed multimodal safety asymmetry, where visual alignment introduces uneven safety constraints across modalities and weakens overall robustness. We analyze attention dynamics and latent representations in MLLMs, revealing that visual inputs can disrupt cross-modal information flow and reduce the model’s ability to separate benign and malicious intents. Motivated by these findings, we propose PolyJailbreak, which organizes the discovered vulnerabilities into a structured library of reusable Atomic Strategy Primitives to enable step-wise transformations from harmful intents to effective jailbreak inputs. Guided by these primitives, a reinforcement learning-based multi-agent optimization process automatically adapts attacks to the target model without access to internal parameters. Extensive experiments on a wide range of MLLMs demonstrate that PolyJailbreak consistently outperforms state-of-the-art jailbreak baselines, with an average improvement of 18.15% in attack success rate and a success rate exceeding 95% on commercial closed-box models, including GPT-4o and Gemini.

title: Ellipsoid Control: A White-List Jailbreak Defense via Benign Latent Modeling
abstract: Representation engineering (RepE) defenses have shown strong robustness against jailbreak attacks on large language models (LLMs). However, these methods fundamentally rely on block-list supervision: they learn jailbreak-to-refusal activation transformations from harmful or jailbreak data that are inherently incomplete and continuously evolving. Hence, the performance of RepE-based defenses becomes tightly coupled to the quality and coverage of collected harmful samples, leaving models vulnerable to unseen attacks. This reliance also obscures the distinction between defenses that fit known harmful distributions and defenses that protect a benign latent region without estimating the harmful distribution. We adopt the opposite, the white-list perspective, by leveraging the accessibility and abundance of benign data. The goal is to elicit refusal on arbitrary inputs while ensuring that harmless inputs are not falsely rejected. This shifts the core research question to: How can we design a robust benign-latent preservation mechanism such that the benign latent distribution remains intact while refusal is elicited? To answer this, we propose Ellipsoid Control, a test-time defense. It performs projected gradient descent that can elicit refusal on arbitrary inputs, aiming to improve defense effectiveness. At the same time, an anisotropic benign-geometry ellipsoid is fitted from abundant benign data to constrain the update to minimize distortion of the benign latent geometry. This tight constraint helps preserve model utility. Across multiple LLMs, jailbreak attacks, benign tasks, and safety-boundary evaluations, Ellipsoid Control consistently enhances safety while better preserving utility, demonstrating the effectiveness of the white-list approach for jailbreak defense.

title: A Multi-Agent Framework for Step-Level Tool-Call Safety Evaluation in Industrial Control Systems
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed to operate industrial systems through structured tool calls to Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) and Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems interfaces. However, unsafe tool-call behaviors—arising from reasoning errors, contextual prompt injection, or explicit malicious requests—can directly lead to physical damage and safety incidents. Despite recent progress in agent safety, standardized benchmarks for evaluating step-level tool-call safety in industrial environments remain lacking. In this work, we present a guardrail-oriented dataset and benchmark for industrial LLM agents. We propose a three-mode safety taxonomy that distinguishes benign, injected-benign, and malicious requests, capturing both explicit attacks and covert contextual manipulations that induce unsafe behaviors in otherwise legitimate tasks. Based on this taxonomy, we construct a step-level dataset using a fully automated multi-agent pipeline that (i) generates industrial environments and tasks, (ii) injects structured contextual manipulations, (iii) samples tool-call trajectories, and (iv) assigns deterministic safety labels grounded in PLC constraints and industrial safety specifications. We further design a challenging cross-domain benchmark spanning six industrial domains, including water treatment, semiconductor manufacturing, pharmaceutical fermentation, oil refining, nuclear cooling, and food processing. The benchmark enforces domain-specific entity naming, realistic numeric values, and constraint mismatches where physical safety limits are stricter than PLC register bounds, enabling systematic evaluation of guardrail generalization under distribution shift. Experimental results show that strong instruction-tuned LLMs, while effective at handling explicitly malicious requests, struggle to detect unsafe behaviors induced by contextual prompt injection, revealing a critical blind spot in existing safety mechanisms. In contrast, a guardrail model fine-tuned on our dataset demonstrates substantially improved sensitivity to step-level safety violations, particularly in injected-benign scenarios, while maintaining robust performance against explicit attacks. These findings highlight the necessity of step-level supervision and the effectiveness of the proposed benchmark for developing reliable industrial agent guardrails. Our dataset and benchmark provide a standardized testbed for step-level tool-call safety in industrial LLM agents and establish a foundation for future research on safe and reliable autonomous industrial systems.

title: An Edge–Cloud Collaborative Framework for Latency Optimization in Prompt Injection Defense
abstract: Prompt injection is a major input-side risk in Large Language Model (LLM) services. In edge-cloud deployments, a natural design is to let the edge perform lightweight detection and send hard-to-judge requests to the cloud for stronger checking. However, when many such requests are forwarded, cloud-side checking itself can become a queueing bottleneck, substantially increasing end-to-end delay, especially tail latency under heavy load. This paper studies how edge-side risk stratification can be used to decide which requests should receive further cloud-side checking, without scaling the provisioned cloud checking tier. We deploy a lightweight edge detector to divide requests into low-, medium-, and high-risk groups. High-risk requests are blocked at the edge, low-risk requests proceed directly, and medium-risk requests are selectively sent to the cloud or downgraded to a restricted execution mode according to both request risk and congestion state. We formulate this process as an online decision problem and show that it is NP-hard. Based on this formulation, we propose Q-TRiG, a low-overhead queue-aware gating policy for medium-risk traffic. Discrete-event simulations show that Q-TRiG reduces cloud queueing delay, suppresses 99th percentile latency spikes, and enlarges the stable operating region under heavy load. The results suggest that risk-stratified selective cloud checking is an effective way to reduce delay in prompt-injection detection pipelines.

title: Trust-Aware Orchestration Architecture for LLM-Assisted Workflows in Multi-Tenant Enterprise Systems
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now call tools and APIs in enterprise systems, creating concrete risks: hallucinated parameters, cross-tenant data leakage, and prompt injection. This paper presents an orchestration architecture for multi-tenant deployments where the LLM proposes actions and a deterministic control plane validates and executes them, organized as three hard enforcement gates (authentication and tenant resolution, role-based tool authorization, and schema validation), four advisory filters (input sanitization, retrieval scoping, execution monitoring, output compliance), and append-only audit logging. The hard gates provide three structural guarantees (tenant isolation, tool-allowlist enforcement, schema conformance) specified as deterministic predicates and verified at the logical control-plane level; they do not defend against within-scope intent manipulation, in which an authorized role invokes an authorized tool with schema-valid parameters for a malicious purpose. A 20-prompt adaptive case study shows within-scope attacks succeed on every one of five LLMs tested, at point-estimate rates of 30%–70%, including the three frontier Claude models (Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4, Opus 4.6). The structural guarantees hold uniformly across 14,885 evaluations: 1,497 custom prompts plus adversarial prompts from two established benchmarks (683 TensorTrust and 777 AgentDojo across three domains and three attack strategies) and a 20-prompt adaptive case study. Targeted attack-success rate on AgentDojo is $\leq 1.9\%$ across all five models, comparable to published defended baselines. Deterministic syntax recovery reduces the 3B model’s false rejection rate from 52% to 15.2% at zero latency cost; frontier models achieve 0%. Input sanitization flagged injection patterns in only 10.2% of injection prompts without solo-rejecting any, confirming pattern-based detection is insufficient. Within-scope intent manipulation remains an open problem the hard gates do not address. The architecture targets enterprise systems requiring explainability, safety, and regulatory compliance.

title: Securing in-Vehicle Large Language Models: A Taxonomy of Integration, Threats, and Trustworthiness
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into in-vehicle systems to support conversational interfaces, diagnostics, and driver assistance. However, the security and safety implications of LLMs operating within the in-vehicle systems remain underexplored. In this paper, we present a taxonomy-driven analysis of in-vehicle LLM integration, categorizing systems by integration depth, modality, and functional role. Using this taxonomy, we identify key threat surfaces and failure modes, including hallucination-induced misguidance, prompt injection, adversarial manipulation, and data leakage. We further examine the challenge of grounding LLM outputs in deterministic control logic, highlighting risks of post-hoc rationalization in safety-critical settings. Based on these insights, we derive design guidelines emphasizing architectural isolation, mediated actuation, and runtime assurance. Our work provides a focused foundation for securing in-vehicle LLM deployments.

title: Study the Effectiveness of Existing Detection Mechanisms Against Prompt Injection in LLMs
abstract: Prompt injection attacks pose a significant security risk to large language models (LLMs) by allowing adversaries to manipulate model behavior through crafted inputs or external context. This paper presents a structured survey and comparative analysis of recent detection mechanisms for prompt injection attacks. Using a systematic review approach, relevant studies from 2023–2025 were identified, screened, and evaluated based on reported metrics, threat models, latency overhead, and deployment constraints. The survey categorizes detection approaches into syntactic, semantic, attention-based, and ensemble methods, highlighting their strengths, limitations, and practical trade-offs. Results show that recent semantic and ensemble detectors achieve high detection rates but often introduce additional latency, while attention-based methods offer deeper insight at the cost of requiring model internals. The paper concludes with best-practice recommendations and key research challenges for developing robust and scalable prompt injection detection strategies.

title: Enterprise Search Portals: Hybrid RAG at Scale for Compliance-Sensitive Knowledge Work
abstract: Enterprise search portals are starting to use large language models to produce direct answers, but regulated advisor workflows need stricter controls than normal chat systems. The system must be fast, must not leak restricted content, and must produce outputs that can be audited. This paper presents a policy-first Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture for enterprise portals at scale. The design combines lexical retrieval (BM25) and dense vector retrieval, enforces access control before any text reaches reranking or generation, fuses rankings using Reciprocal Rank Fusion, and generates answers only from an evidence pack with required citations. We describe the end-to-end architecture, threat model, and security controls for prompt injection and retriever poisoning, along with an evaluation scorecard that reports retrieval quality, answer grounding, hallucination rate, audit coverage, and latency. Experiments on compliance-focused enterprise QA benchmarks show that the proposed approach improves Recall@K and answer accuracy while reducing hallucinations and achieving full audit trace coverage.

title: External Data Extraction Attacks Against Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models
abstract: In recent years, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has emerged as a key paradigm for enhancing large language models (LLMs). By integrating externally retrieved information, RAG alleviates issues like outdated knowledge and, crucially, insufficient domain expertise. While effective, RAG introduces new risks of external data extraction attacks (EDEAs), where sensitive or copyrighted data in its knowledge base may be extracted verbatim by adversaries. These risks are particularly acute when RAG is used to customize specialized LLM applications with private knowledge bases. Despite initial studies exploring these risks, they often lack a formalized framework, robust attack performance, and comprehensive evaluation, leaving critical questions about real-world EDEA feasibility unanswered. In this paper, we present the first comprehensive study to formalize EDEAs against retrieval-augmented LLMs (RA-LLMs). We first formally define EDEAs and propose a unified framework decomposing their design into three components: extraction instruction, jailbreak operator, and retrieval trigger, under which prior attacks can be considered instances within our framework. Guided by this framework, we develop Secret: a Scalable and EffeCtive exteRnal data Extraction aTtack. Specifically, Secret incorporates (1) an adaptive optimization process using LLMs as optimizers to generate specialized jailbreak prompts for EDEAs, and (2) cluster-focused triggering, an adaptive strategy that alternates between global exploration and local exploitation to efficiently generate effective retrieval triggers. Extensive evaluations across 4 models (including 3 leading commercial LLMs) reveal that Secret significantly outperforms previous attacks, and is highly effective against all 16 tested RAG instances. Notably, Secret successfully extracts 35% of the data from RAG powered by Claude 3.7 Sonnet for the first time, whereas other attacks yield 0% extraction. Secret is also evaluated against potential defenses. Our findings call for urgent attention to this concerning yet largely overlooked emerging threat. Code is available here.

title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Transformer Framework for Detecting Adversarial Prompts in Healthcare Chatbots
abstract: Prompt injection attacks is an important security problem in healthcare-specific large language model systems(LLMs). The injected prompt can be used to control the behavior of the model or to leak sensitive data. This vulnerability increases with centralized training pipelines that collect patient prompts on a single server, which leads to data leakage and model poisoning. In this work, we examine Federated Learning (FL) as a privacy-preserving and decentralized prompt injection detection defense for medical chatbots. Using the SPML Healthcare Chatbot Prompt Injection Dataset, we fine-tune a RoBERTa-base classifier in conditions of centralized, IID (Independent and Identically Distributed), federated and Non-IID (Non-Independent and Non-Identically Distributed) federated learning. The experimental results show that the federated model has comparable performance with centralized training, with accuracy of 0.957 and F1-score of 0.964 under IID conditions. The realistic case scenario of Non-IID client distribution was evaluated across 3 different client configurations, the model is able to maintain stable performance with an average performance accuracy of 0.956, precision of 0.942, recall of 0.987, F1-Score of 0.964 and AUC of 0.994. Moreover, the federated setup shows consistent convergence between the communication rounds despite the data heterogeneity. These results suggest that transformer-based federated learning provides an effective and privacy-preserving solution for detecting prompt injection attacks in distributed healthcare conversational AI systems. This work contributes to Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3: Good Health and Wellbeing, SDG 9: Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure, and SDG 16: Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions by enhancing the security and privacy of AI-driven healthcare technologies.

title: Research on Security Enhancement Methods for Adversarial Robust Large Language Model Intelligent Agents for Medical Decision-Making Tasks
abstract: Motivated by the challenge to improve the adversarial robustness, security, and trust of medical decision making intelligent agents, the study developed a full-link security enhancement framework, which describes "input risk perception—medical evidence constraint—knowledge consistency verification—decision confidence reweighting—security output control—adversarial feedback update." The study proposed ARSM-Agent and defined a weighted joint objective consisting of decision accuracy loss, adversarial robustness loss, safety refusal loss, and knowledge consistency loss, with weights of 0.3, 0.3, 0.2, and 0.2, respectively. The whole medical decision formulation is implemented by multi-module collaborative linkage. The study verified that the algorithm can be more efficient than four baselines, including LLM-Agent, Retrieval-Agent, Filter-Agent, and Adv-Train-Agent. Under semantic perturbation, prompt injection, drug-name confusion, and false-evidence attacks, ARSM-Agent reduced the overall attack success rate to 8.7% and achieved a knowledge consistency score of 0.91. Ablation experiments quantified each module’s contribution: removing risk perception, evidence retrieval, consistency verification, and confidence reweighting reduced accuracy by 6.7%, 9.1%, 7.6%, and 4.4%, respectively, and increased attack success rate by 13.8%, 11.1%, 8.6%, and 6.9%. It can solve key security issues of medical Decision Making intelligent agents successfully, obtain secure decision making in challenging scenarios, and give reliable intelligent support to medical decision-making intelligent agents.

title: ShadowCode: Toward (Automatic) External Prompt Injection Attack Against Code LLMs
abstract: Recent advancements have led to the widespread adoption of code-oriented large language models (Code LLMs) for programming tasks. Despite their success in deployment, their security research is left far behind. This paper introduces a new attack paradigm: (automatic) external prompt injection against Code LLMs, where attackers generate concise, non-functional induced perturbations and inject them within a victim’s code context. These induced perturbations can be disseminated through commonly used dependencies (e.g., packages or RAG’s knowledge base), manipulating Code LLMs to achieve malicious objectives during the code completion process. Compared to existing attacks, this method does not necessitate control over the model’s training process, unlike backdoor attacks, and can achieve specific malicious objectives that are challenging for adversarial attacks. Furthermore, we propose ShadowCode, a simple yet effective method that automatically generates induced perturbations based on code simulation to achieve effective and stealthy external prompt injection. ShadowCode designs its perturbation optimization objectives by simulating the victim’s code contexts and employs a greedy optimization approach with two enhancement modules: forward reasoning enhancement and keyword-based perturbation design. We evaluate our method across 13 distinct malicious objectives, generating 31 threat cases spanning three popular programming languages. Our results demonstrate that ShadowCode successfully attacks three representative open-source Code LLMs (achieving up to a 97.9% attack success rate) and two mainstream commercial Code LLM-integrated applications (with over 90% attack success rate) across all threat cases, using only a 12-token non-functional induced perturbation.

title: Intelligent Multi-Agent Reinforcement Sanitizer for Securing LLM Systems
abstract: LMs are increasingly vulnerable to prompt poisoning, where adversarial instructions cause the model to behave unexpectedly. Current defense mechanisms have been inadequate against attacks that are paraphrased or in another language, as well as against multimodal or multi-turn attacks, and generally lack reliable mechanisms for protecting hidden prompts from the system. This paper describes IMARS, a new multi-agent defense pipeline designed to help defend against prompt poisoning of large language models (LLMs). IMARS integrates multiple elements, including semantic contrastive detection, attention-based anomaly scoring, cryptographic integrity verification, iterative sanitization, temporal analysis, and explainability, to form a new pipeline to protect LLMs. IMARS integrates text and OCR inputs to provide multimodal data for the inspection, while also using drift-aware contextual reasoning to detect changes in attack patterns over time. The goal of IMARS is to create a reliable, near real-time, and interpretable security framework that improves LLM safety against sophisticated prompt poisoning attacks while allowing for transparency in the decision-making process. Experimental validation of IMARS effectiveness in the detection and mitigation of sophisticated prompt injection attempts has shown success across a variety of attack conditions.

title: Multimodal Prompt Injection: A Formal 4D Taxonomy for Image and Document Pipelines
abstract: Despite rapid advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), their cross-modal fusion architectures pose significant security concerns. Multimodal prompt injection (MPI) attacks enable adversaries to incorporate malicious instructions within non-textual inputs such as images, PDFs, and slides to manipulate model behavior, bypass controls, and exploit processes such as optical character recognition (OCR) and metadata parsing. Current research is fragmented due to a lack of a cohesive risk classification and consistent evaluation techniques. This paper introduces a formal 4D taxonomy $\mathcal{T}=\langle C, L, O, S\rangle$ that categorizes MPI attacks according to carrier type, pipeline location, attacker objective, and stealth level, resulting in 96 potentially unique attack classes and indicates that merely 7.3% are documented in existing research. Analysis indicates that no singular defense provides comprehensive coverage; a confirmed limit of 75% dimensional coverage is established across all deployable defenders. Layered architectures with provenance and standardized multimodal benchmarks are recognized as critical conditions for effective MPI mitigation.

title: A Systematic Literature Review of Prompt Injection Attacks in LLM-Integrated Systems
abstract: Prompt injection exploits a fundamental property of large language models: the inability to distinguish trusted instructions from untrusted content when both are processed as natural language tokens. As these models are integrated into tool-augmented and memory-enabled systems, the attack surface expands beyond the prompt interface, yet no existing review maps this landscape against standardised adversarial frameworks or analyses the balance between offensive and defensive research. This review follows the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. We searched IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and ScienceDirect for peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and October 2025, yielding 89 included publications of which 81 form the analytical corpus. Aligned to the MITRE Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems framework (version 5.4.0), each paper was coded along three axes: trust boundary, attacker objective, and research orientation with attacker objectives further classified into seventeen operational patterns aligned to MITRE ATLAS techniques. The corpus is dominated by research on the prompt interface and by two attacker objectives, Instruction Hijack and Policy Bypass, leaving underexplored boundaries lacking both attack characterization and defence proposals. This architectural narrowness does not reflect the multi-component architecture of production LLM systems. The three-axis framework and coded corpus establish a baseline for tracking how coverage evolves as deployment architectures expand. The concentration reflects a research incentive structure that favours reproducible prompt-level experiments over architecturally complex assessments at tool and memory boundaries. The field exhibits a maturity gradient in which defence development is concentrated at the prompt interface while other boundaries remain in early or absent characterization. The corpus treats prompt injection as a model-level property rather than a system-level vulnerability.

title: Double-Gaming: Jailbreak Attacks against LLM based on Red-Blue Team Game Theory
abstract: Despite existing security alignment mechanisms, Large Language Models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks under static defenses. To address this, we propose a novel jailbreak attack and defense optimization framework based on Red-Blue Team dynamic game theory. This framework establishes an automated adversarial mechanism between red and blue teams, achieving closed-loop optimization of instruction generation, semantic interception, and strategy evolution. The red team employs reinforcement learning and semantic enhancement techniques to generate highly diverse and concealed adversarial instructions; the blue team constructs a three-tier defense system—"Rule Filtering-Deep Learning-Dynamic Updating"—to enable real-time interception of harmful instructions and continuous model reinforcement. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework achieves significant attack effectiveness across various models including Vicuna-7B, Llama-2-7B, GPT-3.5-turbo, and GPT-4, with a peak Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 98.7%. On the defense side, it reduces the ASR of GCG attacks to 0.9%, validating the efficacy of the dynamic game mechanism in enhancing model robustness.

title: Visual and Structural Prompt Injection in Medical Rag Systems: a Comparative Robustness Analysis
abstract: The integration process of Large Language Models (LLM) into the healthcare ecosystem is demonstrating a shift from cloud-based systems towards local (on-premise) and opensource Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architectures due to data privacy regulations such as GDPR and HIPAA. However, these architectures harbor critical vulnerabilities against indirect prompt injection attacks that target parsing gaps in the document processing layer and manipulate model behavior. In this study, the resilience of 6 distinct local models, including Llama-3, Gemma-3, and Meditron, against visual and structural injection vectors has been quantitatively and qualitatively analyzed. Within the scope of the study, visual-semantic mismatch (white-text), micro-typography, and metadata manipulation techniques were tested on $\mathbf{1 0 0}$ original clinical discharge summaries generated via Google Gemini 2.5 Flash and dynamic prompt engineering. In the threat model, the objective was to have the model diagnose a false septic shock and prescribe meropenem, a high-risk antibiotic with no clinical indication, by suppressing a stable patient profile (context suppression). Analyses involving a total of 2,400 unique experimental steps revealed that standard RAG parsers failed to detect visual payloads hidden from human perception, and the models could be manipulated with an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 47.78 %. The most significant finding of the study is the security asymmetry between models. While the generalpurpose Gemma-3 model exhibited the highest vulnerability with 96.33 % ASR, the Meditron-7B model, trained specifically for the medical domain, demonstrated superior resistance with 8.67 % ASR. The results indicate that domain-specific training establishes a natural security shield (inherent robustness) against injection attacks. On the other hand, the use of general-purpose models in clinical decision support processes without visual sanitization mechanisms poses serious risks in terms of patient safety.

title: Zero-trust Conceptual Architecture for Secure Integration of Large Language Models and Autonomous AI Agents
abstract: The rapid transition from passive large language models to autonomous agent-based coding systems, including frameworks like Claude Code and OpenClaw, has significantly accelerated software development cycles while simultaneously complicating the enterprise attack surface. Conventional security paradigms relying on perimeter defenses and static role-based access control (RBAC) are inherently designed for deterministic entities, leaving them critically underequipped to mitigate threats posed by non-deterministic algorithmic agents. These autonomous systems frequently generate unpredictable, multi-step sequences of system calls upon ingesting poisoned external environment data or hidden prompt injections. This article proposes a novel Zero Trust architectural framework, complete with rigorous mathematical formalization, specifically engineered for secure multi-agent ecosystems. The architectural core features an intelligent Semantic Gateway deeply integrated with operating system-level coordination modules to dynamically provision ephemeral sandboxing environments. To achieve continuous authorization for asynchronous transactions, the framework utilizes a mathematical structure based on Heterogeneous Graph Neural Networks (HGNN). This algorithm continuously computes an agent's dynamic trust tensor by quantifying the topological divergence between its predicted and actual traversal paths within the deterministic space of a corporate repository graph. To empirically validate the analytical efficacy of this advanced architecture, the research team executed a large-scale simulation processing 100,000 asynchronous transactions. The proposed framework demonstrated exceptional predictive power, achieving a true positive rate (TPR) exceeding 98.7 % in the detection and preventive isolation of critical remote code execution vulnerabilities, including sophisticated CVE-2025-61260 exploits. Crucially, this robust security posture was maintained with a minimal false positive rate (FPR) of 1.1 % and an average processing overhead of just 45 milliseconds. Ultimately, this paradigm modernizes the NIST SP 800-207A standard by replacing static binary access controls with a continuous Markov decision process, transforming stochastic AI unpredictability into a quantifiable engineering asset for critical infrastructures.

title: Detection of Prompt Attacks in LLMs
abstract: LLMs (Large Language Models) used in practical implementations have been identified to be very vulnerable to direct prompt injection attacks: when hostile users trigger LLMs by providing input that leads to the LLM ignoring its own instruction and safety protocols/settings. LLMs with existing solutions meant to mitigate prompt injection from being successful, such as static filters and single-stage classifiers, would not be effective against obfuscated, adaptive, and multi-turn prompt injection attacks. This paper describes a new technique called Adversarial Robust Multi-layer Training (ARM-LT) which is real-time, model-agnostic, and designed to detect direct prompt injections at the prompt level. It uses structural prompt segmentation, canonical rewriting of multi-turn prompts, and perplexity based anomaly detection to identify hidden malicious intent before executing the LLM. The ARM-LT framework uses an iterative adversarial training loop in order to provide added robustness to the detection system against adaptive attackers by repeatedly reinforcing the detection system with semantically based adversarial prompt injection attempts. Evaluated a dataset with 78,558 direct prompt injection samples across 6 domains, ARM-LT produces significantly lower attack success rates than traditional machine learning baselines and also supports low inference overhead. This evidence shows that the need for dedicated security layers is critical to ensuring prompt injection is reliably prevented in any LLM integrated system.

title: Behind the Prompt: Privacy Risks in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMS) are progressively adopted since their inception yielding tremendous impact in domains such as finance, healthcare, and cybersecurity. However, they also introduce new vulnerabilities as well among them privacy of the underlying sensitive data is very alarming. This paper explores the problem of data privacy by performing theoretical threat modeling as well as providing an experimental validation. We develop a custom LangChain-based local LLM agent to simulate a controlled environment for testing responses to sensitive, adversarial, and benign prompts. Our analysis considers passive threats, such as data memorization, and active adversarial attacks, including prompt injection and training data extraction. A variety of privacy-preserving methodologies are evaluated in comparison to proprietary models such as OpenAI’s GPT-4o. Finally, we propose a conceptual framework for mitigating privacy risks in practical LLM deployments.

title: MPDA: Multimodal Prompt Decoupling Attack on the Safety Filters in Text-to-Image Models
abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models have been widely applied in generating high-fidelity images across various domains. However, these models may also be abused to produce Not-Safe-for-Work (NSFW) content via jailbreak attacks. Existing jailbreak methods primarily manipulate the textual prompt, leaving potential vulnerabilities in image-based inputs largely unexplored. Moreover, text-based methods face challenges in bypassing the model’s safety filters. In response to these limitations, we propose the Multimodal Prompt Decoupling Attack ($\mathsf {MPDA}$MPDA), which utilizes image modality to separate the harmful semantic components of the original unsafe prompt. $\mathsf {MPDA}$MPDA follows three core steps: firstly, a large language model (LLM) decouples unsafe prompts into pseudo-safe prompts and harmful prompts. The former are seemingly harmless sub-prompts that can bypass filters, while the latter are sub-prompts with unsafe semantics that trigger filters. Subsequently, the LLM rewrites the harmful prompts into natural adversarial prompts to bypass safety filters, which guide the T2I model to modify the base image into an NSFW output. Finally, to ensure semantic consistency between the generated NSFW images and the original unsafe prompts, the visual language model generates image captions, providing a new pathway to guide the LLM in iterative rewriting and refining the generated content. Extensive experiments empirically demonstrate that $\mathsf {MPDA}$MPDA outperforms the baseline methods in two attack scenarios across Stable Diffusion 3.5 and three commercial models: CogView, Tongyiwanxiang, and Midjourney. Specifically, in the pornographic content attack scenario with Midjourney as the victim model, our method has a 29% higher bypass rate than the previous method, thereby providing robust empirical evidence supporting the effectiveness and generalizability of $\mathsf {MPDA}$MPDA. title: RAG-Induced Failures in Multi-Agent Large Language Model Debate
abstract: Multi-agent Large Language Model (LLM) systems based on collaborative debate have been proposed to improve reasoning accuracy and robustness by aggregating diverse reasoning trajectories. However, most debate frameworks implicitly assume that all participating agents behave honestly. This paper demonstrates that this assumption fails under a realistic threat model in which a single malicious agent manipulates Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to selectively retrieve externally sourced evidence that plausibly supports an incorrect conclusion. Unlike prior work that relies on prompt injection or complex persuasion pipelines, the proposed attack requires only retrieval control and uses legitimate documents whose relevance is strategically overstated or misinterpreted. Experiments on TruthfulQA, MMLU, MedMCQA, and SCALR show that RAG-based attacks can reduce majority-vote accuracy by up to 38% while increasing group consensus around false answers. These results indicate that retrieval-often used to improve factual grounding-can instead amplify misinformation when adversarially controlled, motivating stronger verification and trust calibration in multi-agent LLM systems.

title: A Secure Retrieval-Augmented LLM Framework for Cloud-Based Incident Response
abstract: The response to a cloud incident is characterized by the need to make fast decisions and maintain evidentiary integrity, tenant isolation, and adherence to policies. In this paper, the authors introduce SRAG-IR, a secure retrievalaugmented LLM framework governing an incident response on the cloud that interconnects a controlled evidence lake and an attested retrieval and action layer. SRAG-IR builds a timeindexed part of incident memory over logs, alerts, tickets, and certified threat intelligence and determines only those fragments that are policy authorized through attribute-based access control and tenant-bound vector indices. A context firewall removes untrusted instructions in text accessed and enforces schema constrained prompts to minimize prompt injection and data exfiltration. Chunks of evidence are hash-chained and signed and produce verifiable cites and auditable respondent provenance. To have containment and recovery, sandboxed tool broker runs approved cloud actions as per playbook templates, producing change plans and rollback hints. The design enhances trust, privacy, and operational safety and does not need model retraining with multi-tenant production clouds. Dual retrieval integrates semantic search and asset-dependency graphs allowing root-cause hypothesis and prioritized triage suggestions should there be strict latency and cost budget limits.

title: EVA: Editing for Versatile Alignment Against Jailbreaks
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities but remain vulnerable to jailbreaking attacks, where adversaries exploit textual or visual triggers to bypass safety guardrails. Recent defenses typically rely on safety fine-tuning or external filters to reduce the model’s likelihood of producing harmful content. While effective to some extent, these methods often incur significant computational overheads and suffer from the safety utility trade-off, degrading the model’s performance on benign tasks. To address these challenges, we propose EVA (Editing for Versatile Alignment against Jailbreaks), a novel framework that pioneers the application of direct model editing for safety alignment. EVA reframes safety alignment as a precise knowledge correction task. Instead of retraining massive parameters, EVA identifies and surgically edits specific neurons responsible for the model’s susceptibility to harmful instructions, while leaving the vast majority of the model unchanged. By localizing the updates, EVA effectively neutralizes harmful behaviors without compromising the model’s general reasoning capabilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EVA outperforms baselines in mitigating jailbreaks across both LLMs and VLMs, offering a precise and efficient solution for post-deployment safety alignment.

title: Security Issues and Evaluation of Large-Scale Inference Models: An In-Depth Analysis Based on Long Chain-of-Thought
abstract: The integration of large language models into critical applications has introduced significant security vulnerabilities, particularly prompt-based attacks that exploit the coupling of user inputs with system instructions. This paper systematically evaluates prompt attack methodologies and safety risks in large reasoning models (LRMs) with long chain-of-thought (CoT) capabilities. Using the SafeChain framework, we design three reasoning control strategies—ZeroThink, LessThink, and MoreThink—to investigate the relationship between reasoning depth and model safety on the StrongReject-Small dataset across multiple models. Our results demonstrate that extended reasoning does not inherently threaten or enhance safety; rather, its impact is determined by underlying alignment strength. Weakly aligned models exhibit amplified jailbreak success rates under deeper reasoning, while strongly aligned models maintain stable or improved safety through self-scrutiny. Lightweight models face systemic risks including contextual drift. We propose a defense framework incorporating real-time thought monitoring and process-supervised alignment to guide the development of robust safety mechanisms for next-generation reasoning systems.

title: Dual-space Sparse Mask Injection: A Defense Framework for Large Language Models Against Jailbreak Attacks
abstract: Jailbreak attacks compromise the safety of large language models (LLMs) by inducing harmful behaviors through adversarially crafted prompts, often without explicit toxic language. Recent studies show that such attacks operate by perturbing internal representations that mediate refusal and safety-aligned behaviors. However, existing latent-space defenses typically rely on a single semantic direction, which is insufficient to capture the diverse and obfuscated semantics used in jailbreak prompts. We propose Dual-space Sparse Mask Injection (DSMI), a representation-level defense that models jailbreak behavior in two disentangled latent subspaces: a toxicity subspace encoding sensitivity to harmful content and a jailbreak subspace capturing compliance shifts under adversarial prompting. DSMI constructs sparse masks in both subspaces via contrastive representation analysis and intervenes during inference by simultaneously enhancing toxicity-aware features and suppressing jailbreak-induced activation patterns.We evaluate DSMI on multiple jailbreak benchmarks and three open-source LLMs, showing that it substantially reduces attack success rates against both token-level and semantic jailbreak methods while preserving benign task performance. Further analysis demonstrates that the two subspaces are nearly orthogonal and that dual-space intervention provides significantly stronger robustness than single-space latent defenses. These results suggest that disentangling and manipulating multiple safety-relevant representational subspaces is an effective strategy for defending LLMs against adversarial jailbreak attacks.

title: Temporal Dynamics of Memory Poisoning in Web3-Style LLM Agents
abstract: Memory-enabled large language model (LLM) agents, particularly those deployed in long-horizon, tool-using settings such as Web3-style autonomous workflows, introduce security risks that extend beyond single-prompt injection. By persisting and reusing information across interaction steps and sessions, these agents enable memory poisoning attacks in which adversarial inputs modify persistent agent state and influence future decisions after benign intermediate interactions. Recent work on context manipulation and “fake memories” demonstrates that adversarial content can be injected into an agent’s prompt-visible inputs or persistent memory; however, existing evaluations largely analyze such attacks at isolated interaction steps or static context snapshots, obscuring their temporal dynamics. In this paper, we present the first large-scale, trajectory-level measurement framework for analyzing temporal memory poisoning in memory-enabled LLM agents. We construct a schema-constrained dataset of 2,614 multi-step attack trajectories spanning four attack families, chain poisoning, policy rewriting, backdoor triggering, and slow drift, executed over shared persistent memory. We define temporal risk metrics over multi-step interaction trajectories that capture delayed activation, non-monotonic escalation, and the earliest point at which attacks become distinguishable from benign behavior. Our empirical results show that a substantial fraction of attacks remain indistinguishable from benign behavior until late-stage activation, despite exhibiting low or medium risk at all earlier steps. Slow-drift and backdoor-trigger attacks, in particular, systematically evade step-local evaluation until terminal interactions, while chain poisoning and policy rewriting exhibit non-monotonic risk trajectories. These findings demonstrate that memory poisoning risk is inherently temporal and cannot be reliably assessed using prompt-level or step-isolated evaluation, motivating trajectory-aware benchmarks for agent security.

title: Enterprise Secure AI Execution Engine: A Zero-Trust Security Gateway for Enterprise LLM Systems
abstract: Organizations are increasingly adopting Large Language Models (LLMs) for automated decision-making and employee support and secure handling of sensitive organizational data. The systems enabled by these technologies deliver substantial business productivity gains. The systems create major security problems because their implementation enables users to conduct prompt injection attacks and data exfiltration and privilege escalation and adversarial manipulation and policy override attacks. LLM systems operate through natural language interactions which create particular security problems because standard security methods cannot stop attackers who use designed prompts to access LLM systems. The paper introduces an Enterprise Secure AI Execution Engine which functions as a Zero-Trust AI Security Gateway that protects enterprise LLM deployments through its security framework. The proposed architecture combines multiple security mechanisms which include Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) and Data Loss Prevention (DLP) and adversarial prompt detection and deterministic tokenization to create a security system that enforces stringent access protection rules. The system considers all incoming user data to be untrusted and it requires several security checks before permitting model operation. The system demonstrated its capability to identify adversarial prompts while safeguarding sensitive data with minimal effect on processing efficiency. The results demonstrate the system effectively blocks major security threats while it maintains strong defenses against unauthorized data extraction attempts. The proposed framework establishes a secure deployment architecture for enterprise LLM systems and it works best for organizations that need to protect their most sensitive operations.

title: PRISM: Prompt Red-teaming and Injection Simulation for Models – A Scalable Framework for Evaluating LLM Robustness Against Malicious Prompts
abstract: The rapid growth in the adoption of Large Language Models has brought with it some significant security vulnerabilities-one of which is prompt injection attacks. These attacks manipulate the behavior of LLMs using malicious user input, leading to the compromise of system integrity and the production of unintended or harmful output. Traditional detection approaches often cannot keep pace with the complexity and diversity of such attacks. We address this gap by presenting PRISM-Prompt Red-teaming and Injection Simulation for Models-a scalable framework designed to comprehensively assess the robustness of LLMs against adversarial prompts in a systematic manner. PRISM leverages a distributed computing architecture, utilizing Hadoop MapReduce and Ollama, to automatically assess LLM responses against a wide range of prompt variations, along with temperature configurations. It computes similarity-based measures from the large corpus of known prompt injection attempts that PRISM will process to describe model performance and identify successful attack vectors. The proposed work outlines the architecture of PRISM, reports on some initial exploratory data analysis of the HackAPrompt dataset, and demonstrates the ability of the framework to provide a complete, scalable, and automated solution for both LLM security auditing and red-teaming.

title: Two-Layer Input Filtering Framework for Large Language Model Security
abstract: GPT-4 and Mistral (Large Language Model) have strong language performance, but they are still susceptible to being hacked because of prompt injections, jailbreaking, or inappropriately using a playacting role in order to gain access to the LLM's built-in protections. Existing defenses are mainly closed, hard to test, and lack flexibility for being modified by any given deployment configuration. This paper presents a framework based on a modular system of two components: the pre-filtering of input, and the filtering of harmful patterns through the first module using regular expressions and the second by using heuristics to evaluate semantic or intonation meaning to discover other forms of threat. The framework supports deployment with mock models, Hugging Face transformers, and OpenAI APIs. Experiments with curated datasets show over 80% of malicious prompts are blocked, while false positives stay under 10%. The average filter-only latency remains low, between 15 and 20 milliseconds. This system offers a transparent, low-overhead baseline for secure LLM use and lays the groundwork for future research on adaptable, interpretable defenses.

title: Defensive Architectures for LLM-Based Fraud Detection Against Data Poisoning and Prompt Injection
abstract: The increasing adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) in financial fraud detection has enhanced institutional capabilities for identifying sophisticated and dynamic fraudulent activities within large-scale transaction systems. However, the implementation of LLM-driven systems introduces critical security vulnerabilities, particularly data poisoning during training and prompt injection attacks during inference, which threaten the reliability and integrity of automated fraud detection. This paper proposes a Resilient Defensive Architecture for LLMbased Fraud Detection (RDA-LLM), a multi-layered framework designed to protect against adversarial manipulation while maintaining high detection accuracy. The proposed architecture integrates data sanitization, semantic prompt purification, auxiliary adversarial detection, ensemble-based validation, and uncertainty-aware decision gating into a unified defensive framework. Extensive experiments on the Kaggle Credit Card Fraud Detection dataset demonstrate that RDA-LLM outperforms state-of-the-art LLM-based fraud detection models, including LLM40FD and LLM-MalDetect, across several key performance measures such as accuracy, precision, recall, false positive rate, and resistance to adversarial attacks. The results confirm that RDA-LLM provides enhanced resilience without prohibitive inference latency overhead, making it suitable for realtime deployment. This work contributes to enhancing the stability, security, and technological advancement of U.S. financial systems by developing secure, reliable, and scalable solutions that mitigate critical security vulnerabilities in LLM-based systems.

title: Reliability Risk in LLM-Driven Robotic Control
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted to generate operation plans and control code for robotic systems. While the usage of LLMs facilitates the control and operation of robotic systems, it also introduces additional reliability and safety concerns. This article identifies a new angle to explore potential reliability risks of LLM-driven robot control that has safety verification modules integrated. Specifically, this article introduces a red-teaming framework that jailbreaks LLM-driven robotic control systems by exploiting implicit channels in robot operation code, including structured comments and deceptive variable naming. An experimental case study using LLM-driven UAV control tasks is performed with six categories of safety constraints. The results show that auxiliary semantic channels that do not affect execution can still significantly influence safety reasoning and cause reliability risks.

title: Hold the Prompt (HODPOT): Defense Design for Securing the System Prompt of LLM Agents
abstract: Since the public release of ChatGPT, generative AI (GenAI) models have become increasingly functional and autonomous, spurring their integration into a wide range of products. This integration introduces substantial security risks, most notably prompt-injection attacks that can manipulate model outputs and expose proprietary data. A less-studied variant—prompt-theft, where an adversary who fully controls the user prompt extracts the system prompt or a semantically equivalent paraphrase—remains viable even against state-of-the-art models. We formalise this threat under an attacker model that can issue arbitrary user inputs and observe the model’s responses. Our defense is a lightweight post-inference similarity filter: each generated output is compared using text similarity measures with a calibrated threshold that determines whether the response is returned unchanged, sanitized, or blocked. Experiments on eight LLMs and two “guard”-type models show that the filter reduces successful prompt extraction two-third of occurences while preserving above $90 \%$ of benign responses. These findings, given the the increasing usage of fully-autonomous GenAI agents, re-highlight prompt theft as a pressing research problem and motivate further work on adaptive thresholds, multi-modal prompts, and compositional leakage.

title: Beyond Shared Embedding Spaces: Towards LLM Architectures with Explicit Authority Control for Prompt Security
abstract: Large Language Models are highly susceptible to prompt injection because their architecture fails to separate system instructions from untrusted user data. Current defenses offer only superficial mitigation by addressing symptoms, not the root cause. This paper proposes a fundamental architectural shift to enforce this separation through mechanisms like authority-aware attention and segregated processing pathways. We outline existing vulnerabilities and present an architectural roadmap towards next-generation LLMs with structurally enforced instruction integrity and inherent resilience against prompt injection.

title: Comprehensive Analysis of LLM Guardrails Approaches Preventing Harmful Content and Jailbreak Attacks
abstract: LLMs (Large Language Models) have become increasingly important, with chatbots being widely used in commercial settings to assist employees and answer customer questions. To protect a company’s reputation and ensure compliance, it’s crucial that chatbots do not generate harmful content, even in the face of deliberate jailbreak attacks. Researchers propose various methods to secure LLMs, known as guardrails, to prevent harmful content generation and jailbreak attacks. This article aims to comprehensively analyze existing guardrail solutions and provide guidelines for selecting the optimal solution for specific scenarios. The study compared six different guardrail methods across three versions of LLMs (Mistral Large 24.02, Meta Llama 3-8B Instruct, Anthropic Claude 3.5 Sonnet), including two baseline approaches, two cloud-based solutions (AWS Guardrails, Azure AI Content Safety), and two other popular non-cloud solutions (NeMo by Nvidia and Llama Guard by Meta). Thirteen datasets were used for evaluation: ten representing harmful questions in jailbreak attacks and three with neutral prompts similar to harmful questions to check for excessive blocking. The best results were achieved by AWS Guardrails (averaged accuracy across models 96.8%) and NeMo (93.9%) The results clearly showed that using guardrails is essential when building commercial applications based on LLMs due to advancements in effective jailbreak attacks.

title: PromptFence: A Semantic Guardrail for Healthcare AI to Defend Against Prompt Injection Attacks
abstract: The use of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly growing in healthcare to perform valuable tasks, including summarizing clinical notes, extracting vital signs, and translating medical language. However, there is a serious patient safety and confidentiality risk associated with a user engaging in a prompt injection-a malicious instruction hidden in the input. In light of this challenge, we are introducing the concept of PromptFence, which is a semantic guardrail that captures and analyzes prompts before entering the core LLM. Using BERT-base embeddings and contrastive loss-based intent similarity, PromptFence checks inputs for alignment with an approved set of healthcare tasks and flags or sanitizes instructions that do not align with the safe intent of the task, or worse, are malicious.

title: Parallel Hybrid Classical-Quantum Architecture for AI Safety and LLM Jailbreak Detection
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly vulnerable to adversarial "jailbreak" attacks designed to elude safety and privacy controls. Detection is still a challenging task due to the complexity of adversarial prompts and labeled data scarcity. While fine-tuning a traditional Transformer model, such as BERT and its variants, provides strong backbone results with frequently limited recall of complex edge cases, it often comes with extensive computational costs. This work proposes a parallel hybrid classical-quantum architecture. Unlike previous serial approaches which constraint information through a quantum circuit, the proposed model uses an ensemble of a classical multilayer perceptron and a data re-uploading quantum circuit, working in parallel on top of a partially unfrozen BERT backbone. Results on the Jailbreak Classification task show that this indeed provides promising results by serving as a residual correction mechanism. The proposed parallel model achieves an F1-score of 0.911 and an accuracy of 0.910, outperforming the fully fine-tuned classical BERT baseline by over 3%. Apart from the hybrid model, several Serial Variational Quantum Circuit (VQC) arrangements have been considered. These lightweight quantum-only classifiers achieve results comparable to the classical baseline across various metrics by only using a few thousand trainable parameters and operating on heavily compressed BERT embeddings. What is more important is that this emphasizes the fact that compact quantum circuits can outline meaningful decision boundaries under extreme dimensionality constraints. Therefore, such quantum components can reinforce the efficiency and scalability perspective as modules for the safety-focused monitoring of LLMs systems.

title: Evaluating LoRA Adaptation and Fine-Tuning for Multi-Class Adversarial Prompt Detection in Transformer Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have changed the way we interact with AI, but their openness also makes them vulnerable to malicious prompt attacks. Two of the most common threats are jailbreak attacks, where users trick models into bypassing safety filters, and prompt injection attacks, where hidden instructions are inserted into otherwise normal text. Detecting these adversarial prompts is challenging because attacks evolve at a fast pace and appear benign at first sight. In this work, we explore how different supervised fine-tuning strategies affect the ability of transformer models to detect such types of attack. We compare LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning on Google’s Gemma2B, Microsoft’s Phi-2 and TinyLlama with full fine-tuning of smaller transformer models like BERT-base, mDeBERTa and DistilBERT. Our dataset takes examples from several widely used datasets, including JailBreakV-28K, TrustAIRLab’s In-the-Wild Jailbreak Prompts and deepset/prompt-injections, covering three categories: benign, prompt injection, and jailbreaking. We have found LoRA-tuned Gemma-2B, TinyLlama and Phi2 performs competitively with fully fine-tuned BERT models while training only at fractions (less than 1%) of parameters. This shows that LoRA fine-tuning can maintain strong detection performance while reducing the computational cost significantly in large models, making it a practical solution for improving the safety of language models while keeping the base model weights freezed and still usable for general tasks like generating explanations for the detection. Our findings suggest that efficient supervised fine-tuning techniques like LoRA can help build faster, efficient, and scalable defense systems against evolving jailbreak and prompt injection attacks.

title: Is GenAI the Holy Grail of Technology?
abstract:
Summary

This chapter focuses on the accessibility of the new technology and considers the Gartner hype cycle. The Gartner curve, also known as the hype cycle, summarizes the phases of enthusiasm experienced by a technology. It is structured into five phases: Innovation or Technology Trigger; Peak of Inflated Expectations; Trough of Disillusionment; Slope of Enlightenment; and Plateau of Productivity. Generative AIs can generate two types of hallucinations. The University of Hong Kong published an article in February 2023 about a relevance test researchers conducted on ChatGPT. Jailbreaking demonstrates that human language—the “intelligent” language—is far more powerful than any frameworks we can impose, because humans can always find a way around them by being just a little bit smarter than the machine. Open source refers to the willingness of certain developers of applications and software to provide free access to the source code of their product.

title: The Generative AI Attack Surface
abstract:
Summary

This chapter explores the unique and expanding attack surface of generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems, particularly large language models, highlighting how their architectural design introduces vulnerabilities distinct from traditional predictive models. By examining key components such as transformer attention mechanisms, token embeddings, autoregressive output patterns, and contextual conditioning, the chapter reveals how adversaries can exert influence without needing access to source code or system internals. The inherent flexibility and openness of generative outputs make these systems highly susceptible to manipulation through subtle prompt engineering, data poisoning, and internal activation triggers.

The chapter also delves into the risks posed by retrieval‐augmented generation (RAG) systems, where external documents are dynamically incorporated into model context during inference. These integrations open the door to indirect prompt injection, corpus poisoning, and semantic redirection—often without triggering visible model misbehavior during standard evaluations. Fine‐tuning, especially when performed with unvetted or third‐party data, is shown to be a powerful vector for embedding persistent backdoors and trigger‐based behaviors that evade traditional QA processes but remain reliably exploitable in production environments.

For professionals securing AI applications, this chapter reframes the threat model around generative systems as a dynamic behavioral risk, not just a static software flaw. It emphasizes the importance of understanding internal model structures, context‐aware manipulation techniques, and adversarial testing that mirrors how attackers condition models across time, input structure, and retrieved data. With clear analysis and applied framing, this chapter equips readers to identify, evaluate, and begin defending against the behavioral exploits that define modern generative AI threats.
